subtopic: RECRUITING OF WOMEN FOR REGULAR AND RESERVE FORCES
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Has the minister's attention been called to a press dispatch carried in the Montreal Gazette this morning to the effect that his department intends to organize a women's division in the R.C.A.F.? If that is correct, will the minister indicate why these announcements are not made to the house rather than to the press?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxlon (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: RECRUITING OF WOMEN FOR REGULAR AND RESERVE FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the first question, as to whether my attention has been called to this press dispatch, is yes. The answer to the second question, as to whether it is in accordance with the intention of the department, it is partly so, and I shall explain that in a moment. The third question was: Why are these announcements not made to the House of Commons rather than through press statements? Whenever it is possible they are made to the House of Commons. There was no announcement made through any press statement, but there was some intelligent
speculation on the part of the press, based on an article in an R.C.A.F. publication, which was prepared even before the decision had been made to have some women in the armed forces.
My intention was to make a statement about this when the defence estimates came up for consideration. Hon. members will recall that the Prime Minister suggested on April 11 that this might take place on April 12, very nearly two weeks ago. I was prepared to make a statement on this subject at that time which would have prevented the intelligent anticipation of this by the press. Since the question has been asked, perhaps I might be permitted to make that statement now, because it is a matter of widespread interest. This is what I had intended to say on April 12:
Experience in the last war demonstrated that there were a number of jobs in the armed forces which could be filled very satisfactorily by women, but it was recognized that there were disadvantages connected with their employment in peacetime in relatively small armed forces. For one thing the career opportunities were not likely to be great enough to attract women having the necessary qualities of leadership to meet a large increase in the event of war.
For this reason following the conclusion of hostilities the women's corps in the Canadian navy, army and air force were not set up as part of the new peacetime forces.
But now, with the expansion of our armed forces, there is a real need for a limited number of women to carry out duties for which they are specially fitted.
In all three services there are a number of such duties which experience has shown can be done as well or better by women than by men. Clerks and stenographers are obvious illustrations. There is also a whole new group of occupations related to radar and communications. Ground control of ships or aircraft or anti-aircraft guns requiring the use of radar involves, in addition to the operators themselves, personnel to compute the course of the moving ships or aircraft. Moreover, today practically all non-operational telecommunications are carried on by teletype. Active and reserve units are hooked up in nation-wide networks involving the employment of large numbers

Inquiries of the Ministry of skilled personnel. A large part of this work can be very well done by women.
Further, in the event of a general war, manpower shortages would make it essential to employ women on an even larger range of duties in the armed forces for which it would be desirable now to have a relatively small nucleus.
Accordingly, we have decided to recruit a limited number of women for the regular air force and for the reserve forces of the navy, army and air force.
It is not expected that there will be separate corps or establishments for women at the outset. In a unit or formation they will fill a place normally filled by a man.
No women will be enlisted to do clerical work at headquarters. So far as possible we will continue to have this work done by civilians.
It is expected that recruiting will commence this summer.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, April 23, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in dealing with this budget and the amendments to the motion now before us, I am sure that all members of the house-and I am confident I speak at least for all members of the official opposition-adopt as their basic approach to this problem the theme that essential expenditures must be met out of current revenues, which means by current
The Budget-Mr. Fulton taxes, and that therefore if high taxes are necessary, they must be imposed and will be borne by the Canadian people; but that when we are pressed as we are now-at least with respect to those in the lower income groups- to a point close to the limit of the load we can bear, then we must choose between luxuries and extravagance in government spending or higher taxes. In other words, as to those expenditures that can be eliminated, even though we might in normal times like to have them made, if they can be eliminated without interfering with essential services or construction programs, they must go.
In the light of that main theme, I find two main criticisms of this present budget. The first is that to increase taxes to the extent to which they have been imposed in the budget is unnecessary. It is unnecessary to increase taxes to this point; because the government has failed miserably in attacking this problem of reducing non-essential expenditures with any attitude of determination, and has failed almost completely, having regard to results, with respect to the elimination of unnecessary, unproductive and wasteful expenditures. The result has been that when we continue these expenditures at the present level and are faced with the necessity of increasing expenditures for defence preparedness, taxes are unnecessarily high. The second criticism of the budget is that the tax increases that have been provided are in large part inflationary.
Turning to the first head of this criticism in some detail, I would start with a question: How can this government, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who so readily asks the people of Canada to cut down on their luxuries and on their luxury spending-even taxes the people on what they spend on necessities through sales and excise taxes- how can they have the effrontery to continue at the present level their own enormous expenditures on luxuries and non-essentials? Let us look at some of the totals of government spending.
These totals that I shall give are all exclusive of figures for national defence and defence production. The tables are taken from the table which the Minister of Finance included as a supplement to the estimates which he brought down this year. We find that, leaving out civil salaries and wages and civilian allowances, and excluding national defence and defence production-the figures are taken to the nearest hundred thousand dollars-we have the following totals: Professional and special services for this year, $36,000,000 as against $24 million last year; travel and transportation, $13,900,000, an increase from $13,800,000; freight, express,

The Budget-Mr. Fulton etc., $2,300,000 as against $2,100,000; telephones, telegraphs, etc., $4,800,000, an increase from $4,600,000; printing of reports and publications, $3,900,000 as against $4 million; films, displays, advertising, broadcasting, etc., $4,800,000 as against $5 million; office furnishings, stationery and supplies, $11,200,000 as against $11,500,000; materials and supplies, and this is excluding land and buildings -apparently it is office materials and supplies -$39,400,000 as against $37,600,000, and for postage, $3 million in each year. The total, Mr. Speaker, is $109,900,000 for 1951-52 as against $105,600,000 for the last year. Therefore under nine headings alone we have an increase of $4,300,000 this year as against the estimates for a year ago. We are certainly not doing very well in our economy drive, about which the Minister of Finance has said so much.
I challenge anyone, Mr. Speaker, to show that these items that I have listed are all essential. I challenge anyone to maintain that we need the present level of spending on such items as special and professional services, travelling expenses, office equipment, advertising, publicity and displays. These are luxuries, a good part of which at least could be eliminated. I suggest very strenuously again that when the people are required to reduce their level of spending on what the government calls luxuries, although in many instances necessities are taxed-when people are being required to do that, then government as the first measure must reduce its own spending on these luxury items.
But speaking of challenges-and I said I challenge anyone to show that we need the present level of spending on these headings- I should like to refer to a challenge issued by the Minister of Finance last year in his speech on April 28, 1950. When he was closing the budget debate of that year the Minister of Finance used these words, as found on page 1991 of Hansard for that day. He was referring to the letter that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) had written to him suggesting the setting up of a commission to examine government expenditures in Canada and to suggest ways and means of eliminating waste and duplication. The Minister of Finance said:
In his letter my hon. friend has suggested that there exists in the government service waste, extravagance, duplication of services and the like. I categorically challenge that statement: I categorically deny it. In my judgment there is no duplication, waste and extravagance.
Yet the minister in his budget speech this year, and in his baby budget speech last fall, boasted of saving. He says that he has saved $35 million this year. Well, Mr. Speaker, the


question then is, if there was no waste, extravagance or unnecessary spending, how is he able to save any money at all? The minister has said that these savings which he is making are being made without interfering with efficiency and without impairing any necessary program. He says that he has made some savings, in spite of the previous denial that there was any room for saving, but he has saved only a fraction of what he could save, and his total saving amounts to 1.8 per cent of the ordinary expenditures of the government-that is, apart from defence and defence production-or, as was pointed out earlier by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), it amounts to If cents on every dollar that we spend, apart from what we spend on defence.
The parliamentary assistant has repeated the challenge of the Minister of Finance. He repeated it in his speech yesterday, and I am reading now from page 2279 of Hansard:
Early this session I made quite a long speech on this subject.
It is a pity that the results in measures of economy did not equal the length of the parliamentary assistant's speech. He went on to say:
In this house I repeated the challenge to him. I asked for the co-operation of every member of the house in indicating where the savings were to be made . . .
I am glad to take up the challenge of the Minister of Finance and of the parliamentary assistant to suggest concrete savings, although I think we should point out that apparently the parliamentary assistant has not been as observant as he should be, because concrete suggestions have been made in the past. I can only assume that they have been ignored both by the minister and by his assistant.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Such as?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, I will come to them later. The parliamentary assistant knows them already, but I will come to them again for him in a little while. Just before doing so I should like to deal with another statement made by the parliamentary assistant in the course of his speech yesterday. He referred to a technique which he described as the technique of the big lie. I am using his words, Mr. Speaker; they are not mine. His words are to be found at page 2281 of Hansard. He suggested that in maintaining that the government is wasteful and extravagant in its spending habits the official opposition was adopting this technique which he so described, and he criticized us for what he alleged to be a failure to be specific. He repeated the unfounded and unjustified statement that no specific suggestions for savings have been made. All this, he said, amounts to the

technique which he described-with an apparently intimate knowledge of how it works-namely the technique of the big lie.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have listened to it so often.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, you may have listened to it, but you practised it on this occasion rather successfully.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't be too hard on him.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I refute absolutely the statements made by the parliamentary assistant so far as his criticisms of the official opposition are concerned. I say-and I will show-that none of his statements is borne out by an examination of the facts. So that in making his false and misleading assertions he has shown himself a master of the technique he was discussing, namely, the technique of the big lie.
If one analyses the facts one will find they show that we are not the only ones who are saying the government is extravagant and wasteful, although yesterday the parliamentary assistant sought to create the impression that everyone else in Canada is satisfied that the government is exercising the maximum economy, and that only the Progressive Conservative party accuses it of being extravagant. We are not the only ones who say the government has failed to reduce expenditures where they could be reduced. I refer to an editorial in one of the leading papers of this country, which has something to say on the point. Referring to the present level of non-essential or non-defence spending, it says:
There will be distinct gain if, in paying the taxes, the public realizes how essential it is that the government should cut down on non-defence spending. Mr. Abbott had a great deal to say about economy, but the government's achievement here was only $35 million out of $2,036 million, virtually total failure.
Then it goes on to say:
The choice is between necessary defence expenditures and an unnecessarily high level of non-defence spending-between the "pursuit of peace" and skyrocketing prices.
That is an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 2, 1951,-a paper outstanding in its support for the government over the years-commenting on the budget and estimates for this year. So that the official opposition is not the only one that has been making this type of statement.
Secondly, examination of the facts shows that we have been specific in suggesting places where unnecessary expenditures might be eliminated. That was done last year. I myself did it in the course of the budget debate. It was done also in connection with the estimates last year, when we moved
The Budget-Mr. Fulton a reduction in the amount of an item. Hon. members will recall what happened on that occasion, how it was shown quite clearly that the government is not really interested in making a serious study to see whether or not expenses can be reduced. When we did move such a reduction, the impossibility of effecting savings by that method was demonstrated when the government called in all its members, put the issue to a vote as a matter of want of confidence, and defeated the attempt to reduce the expenditure on the basis of a want of confidence motion.
If the parliamentary assistant will examine the facts, and if he will be fair and honest in the matter, he will realize there have been several occasions-many	occasions-when
specific reductions have been suggested, but have been ignored or defeated by the government.
Thirdly, an examination of the facts will show that the parliamentary assistant is himself a past-master at the technique to which he referred; and so, incidentally, perhaps by association, is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), in their habit of making, and repeating without foundation, the assertion that no reduction in expenditures can be made. That assertion was made by the minister on a couple of occasions at least last year, both in the spring and in the fall session; and the whole tenor of the speech yesterday by his parliamentary assistant was to the same effect, that the government is not guilty in any degree of extravagant waste or unnecessary expenditure and that the people of Canada know this fact.
But those statements are without foundation. If we look at some of the examples of government spending we can readily see places where savings can be made. First let us look at some of the increases in government expenditures and government service over the years. I have taken some of these figures from a book by Mr. Taylor Cole, in which appears a study he made and published in 1949 under the title "The Canadian Bureaucracy". In this instance, incidentally, the word "bureaucracy" is used in a non-derogatory sense, and simply as a descriptive word for the whole civil service and public employment set-up in the Dominion of Canada. It is a most impartial and excellent study, and one which contains a good deal of interesting and valuable information. When one compares the figures in Mr. Cole's book as to the number of employees in the government service on the various dates he mentions, with the figures for today, it is easy to see to what an unnecessary extent the government service has been expanded.

The Budget-Mr. Fulton
Let us look at the figures for some of the larger departments. These figures show that the Post Office Department in 1946 had 15,256 employees, whereas, according to the estimates for this year, it now has 17,877. I wonder what tremendously increased services are being given by the Post Office Department to justify this increase in staff of over 2,500 in about four years. Then we see that while in 1946 the Department of Veterans Affairs was able to render a satisfactory service with 12,830 employees, in 1951, when one would have thought the rehabilitation program and the settlement of veterans would be well under way and operating smoothly, the department has a staff of 14,295, or an increase of over 1,400.
The Department of Transport in 1943 was able to get along with 6,273 employees- and that, I would point out was at the peak of the war, when vast quantities of supplies, men and munitions were being moved as part of Canada's war effort. Yet in 1951-52 the estimates for that department show that they require a staff of 10,586, or an increase of more than 4,000 over the number they had in the war years.
In 1939, the latest figure given in Mr. Cole's book for this department, the Department of National Revenue operated with 4,415 men. We certainly realize that the government is collecting much more by way of taxation now than it was in 1939, but I do not see that the personnel of that department need have been expanded to the point where it now numbers 14,024. In other words the Department of National Revenue now has a staff more than three times as large as it did in 1939.
Let us look at the unemployment insurance commission, which carries 7,008 employees to administer the unemployment insurance fund. The administrative costs of the unemployment insurance commission for this year alone amount to $23,700,000. That is a most interesting figure. An examination of the estimates shows that the government's contribution for this year to the unemployment insurance fund	is $27,500,000. The
administrative costs, as I have said, are $23,700,000.	These figures	show
that it is costing us practically as much to administer the fund this year as the government is contributing to the fund. It appears therefore that it requires a staff of 7,000 to look after the approximately
200,000	unemployed at the present time. In other words there is one on the staff for each 35 unemployed persons, and the cost of administration almost equals the annual contribution made by the government. I

suggest that not only is that totally unwarranted, but there is very grave danger to the unemployment insurance fund if these high administrative costs continue at their present level.
To turn to a second phase of unnecessary government spending, one should compare the increases in the estimates this year with last year's level of expenditures. Take civil salaries and wages-again these are exclusive of defence and defence production; here we have an increase of $19,500,000. It must be observed in all fairness that there has been a substantial increase this year in the level of wages.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Ten per cent.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The parliamentary assistant points out that it is ten per cent. I will not make a criticism of that increase, therefore, but simply place it on the record. Then we take civilian allowances, which show an increase this year over last year of $400,000. Professional salaries and special services, about which I shall have something to say a little later, show an increase this year of $2,600,000. Travelling expenses, exclusive of defence and defence production, show an increase of $144,000; freight, express and cartage, an increase of $220,000; telephones, telegrams, etc., $225,000; materials and supplies, $1,800,000.
Looking at those increases alone, we must note that they are increases in ordinary expenditures quite apart from defence and defence production in a year of great stress, and it is surely obvious that a general examination suggests that there is room for economy. Look at some of the specific items which indicate unnecessary expenditure. Let us take the national film board, which shows an amount this year of $2,602,000. Before I proceed I am going to suggest that it is not the primary responsibility of the opposition to do a job which is actually the government's job, that is, to go through the various heads of government expenditure and suggest where reductions can be made; however, the government having thrown out this general and rather meaningless challenge, and the government having failed to make any determined or successful effort to reduce unnecessary and wasteful expenditure, I accept the challenge. It is a pity that it should be left to the opposition to do the government's job, but that being the state of affairs imposed upon us and upon the country by the government, I think the opposition would be failing in its duty to the country if it did not accept the challenge and try to do for the people

the job which the government should be doing for them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was not a challenge; it was a request for co-operation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may be said of the items which I am going to mention that they are desirable heads of expenditure; and if we had lots of money, if we could afford them, if taxes were low, then it is true we might be able to indulge in some of these expenditures without objection. But when we have reached the point where we are now, with inflation and with the cost of living crushing people in the lower income groups, I suggest that the government must decide whether we are going to have savings on these items or are going to continue this unproductive, extravagant and wasteful level of present expenditure.
The national film board is a very nice thing to have around if you have lots of money. If we reduce it by half, we would save $1,301,000. Take all other government publicity and we find that if we can reduce the present rate of expenditures by only half we will save a further $3,054,000. Take the matter of printing departmental reports and other publications, another branch of publicity; if we reduced that by half we would save $3,058,000. Take the matter of office stationery and furnishings. Surely to goodness we must be fairly well along the road to completely equipping the government offices we have at the present time. But if we reduced this by only one-third of the amount the government proposes to spend this year we would save $5,853,000.
Take travelling and removal expenditure, amounting to over $36 million. The Department of National Defence shows a considerable increase under this item, but that does not account by any means for the total. If we saved only one-third it would amount to $12,103,000. Take materials and supplies- and here I exclude defence and defence production. Some materials and supplies are necessary; but do we need the elaborate and expensive and continuous and uncontrolled level of expenditure there is on this type of equipment? If we could save only one-sixth of what we are being asked to spend on materials and supplies, again excluding defence and defence production, we would save $6,556,000.	[DOT]
Next is professional and special services, which covers the payments made to special professional and technical employees outside the civil service. If we were to save one-third of this item it would amount to $12 million. The total savings by the modest
The Budget-Mr. Fulton reductions suggested under all these items would amount to $45 million in a year's operations.
If you look at the table which the Minister of Finance has included with this year's estimates you will find that ordinary expenditures, excluding defence and defence production, show increases in twelve categories as against decreases in only ten. If you include defence and defence production you will find there are increases in nineteen categories as against decreases in only three. That certainly does not suggest any very determined economy drive.
Going back to some of the specific items I have mentioned, in case it may be said that it is all very well to take a general list and indicate what might be saved, I intend to look at these in some detail. Take the matter of government publicity. The parliamentary assistant says that we speak about this in general and are not apt to go into detail. I suggest that the purpose of government publicity, if it has any purpose, is to sell legislation, to sell democracy by showing what democracy does, to publicize what parliament does in the legislation which it passes. Its purpose is not to sell ministers and Liberal policies. But that undoubtedly is one of the main tasks of the government publicity bureaux as they are set up in the different departments at the present time.
I repeat that the only justifiable purpose of government publicity is to sell parliament, legislation and democracy; it should not be used to help ministers vie with one another. That being so, the proper way to handle this would be as we handle other government services, by setting up one publicity bureau to centralize and control this work and the expenditures on it. Specific suggestions to this effect have been made on at least two previous occasions. I challenge the parliamentary assistant, the Minister of Finance or anyone else to show that if you did that and gave that bureau just half the present over-all total for government publicity you would not get a much better and more efficient job.
It is perfectly true that this might hurt some of the advertising firms which get the money now, and then take over the election campaign publicity for the Liberal party when the elections come round; but it
would not hurt anybody else. It would provide legitimate government publicity, which is the only type of publicity on which public money should be spent. If further evidence is needed that government publicity has got out of all bounds, I would refer to

The Budget-Mr. Fulton a Canadian Press dispatch which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of April 21 and which reads:
Publishers of 86 Canadian daily newspapers expressed concern over the growing volume of publicity releases from federal government departments.
Handling of these releases was criticized in resolutions adopted unanimously yesterday at the concluding session of the Canadian Daily Newspapers Association annual meeting.
The reason for this unsatisfactory situation, Mr. Speaker, is that these publicity bureaux in the departments appear to be vying with each other to see if they can build up their minister as the next leader of the Liberal party.
Take the question of professional and special services. Without defence and defence production the estimates this year call for an expenditure of $26,676,000, an increase of $2 million over last year. With defence and defence production they call for a total expenditure of $35 million. Why, one may ask, is this huge amount being spent on professional and special services, paid to people outside the civil service when there are approximately 150,000 civil servants available to the government, 150,000 men and women many of whom are highly paid, and the vast majority of whom are extremely able and capable? Why then must we spend $35 million outside the civil service on professional and special services?
I suggest it is because it affords a very ready and pleasant medium of payment, outside the control of the civil service, to friends of the government. After all, we have had some examples of that. The parliamentary assistant yesterday brought into the debate the name of a gentleman who is at the present time a member of the house when he referred to the present Liberal leader for Ontario and said that he was the man upon whom they relied to flatten the present premier of Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, if the times we live in were different, if there was not such a sense of urgency in the air, I would have asked the indulgence of the house while I spoke of the local problems and hopes of my own people, the 55,000 voters who make up the constituency of Montreal Mount Royal. But I know that I speak for my constituents when I say that this is a time for concentration on the broader and more urgent issues which now confront this nation and the world- rather than to dwell on the particular needs of any one local constituency.
My people are aware of what confronts them on the world scene. They are alert. They want to know about many things- the Atlantic pact, the cost of living, our defence program, our foreign commitments and how much they cost, the reasons for higher taxation. They want to know what they get in return for the moral and financial support they give to the system of government under which we all operate, and which costs like blazes in men, in materials and in money. I have tried to answer these questions, and in trying I have found a certain failure on the part of those of us in Ottawa to communicate fully the facts about where we are leading Canadians; about what we are trying to do, to safeguard their interests and to assure them reasonable security for the future, continued prosperity, and freedom.
I venture to embark on such considerations, as a new member representing a new constituency, a constituency which is so representative of all that is Canada today. Election to this house has placed me in the position

of representing a complete Canada in miniature, a nation in itself, with 55,000 voters in twelve municipal districts, and with population ratios very similar to those of Canada as a whole. All income and social groups are represented in much the same proportions as you will find in the national scene. Mount Royal's minorities include Canadians of all racial origins, with all their individual idiosyncrasies. There are the sedate and wealthy residents of the towns of Montreal West, Hampstead and Mount Royal; up and coming St. Laurent with the largest housing development in the British commonwealth,-Norgate; St. Laurent, where two main language groups work side by side vying with each other in their efforts to create a progressive modern community. At other points in the riding you will find residential areas occupied by industrial workers and certain lower income groups.
When I look at the march of industry into Montreal Mount Royal, I sometimes wonder what the good brothers of the oratory of St. Joseph, that shrine perched on the mountainside, what they must think as they gaze over the vast area below. Here a few short years ago they looked upon green fields as far as the eye could see. Now all is vast housing projects, sprawling busy factories, swarming thoroughfares, whole new industries such as aviation, including Canadair, chemical research, foundries, printers, manufacturers, -nine great hospitals, several famous colleges, a myriad of churches and synagogues. Anyone driving through the riding of Mount Royal cannot miss the feeling of urgency, of progress, of modern Canada that underlies this thriving busy expanding segment of our national economy, my constituency. (Translation):
When speaking of my constituency, it is only fitting that I should take advantage of this first opportunity to thank, in their own language, my 18,000 French-speaking electors for the trust they have placed in me.
I assure them of my entire devotion to their interests.
(Text):
In a battle of ideas such as presently engages mankind, a battle for men's minds in effect, the winner will be he who has the best ideas provided he gets his ideas across best, too. In other words, provided he can communicate his ideas to the people. It is essential, tremendously essential, that our leaders do not withdraw, do not separate themselves from the people. Rather, they must make extraordinary efforts to explain the why and the wherefore of their actions and policies. They must communicate with the people. Can we honestly say that we are winning the war of ideas? Are we con-
The Budget-Mr. Macnaughton centrating enough upon communicating our concepts, our needs, our urgencies to those who look to us for leadership? My experience is that we are not.
Since the beginning of this session the government, with very commendable speed and refreshing frankness, has presented policies of great importance to this house. The thorny "manpower problem" was raised and answered with the greatest honesty by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). A detailed report on "foreign affairs" was made by the minister in charge. An expensive but integrated plan for "national defence" was presented and "stand-by emergency powers" enacted. The creation of a department of "defence production" is now a fact. It is ready to carry out the strengthening and expansion of a whole range of activities that support the defence effort. For unmobilized resources, however vast they may be, do not win wars. And now, the "budget." There is no doubt that the plans and policies of the government have been carefully thought out and carefully presented to this house.
But do the Canadian people understand and appreciate fully the reasons for these great plans-these plans which will almost certainly bring about economic, political and social changes in our normal way of life; these plans which may stay with us for years to come? Is the government doing enough to communicate the purpose and ideas behind the plans of these top-level decisions? While the country is aware in general terms that the world situation is very bad indeed, people do not know in detail what their own part should be. They have just been told firmly what they must do without, but they still, I submit with due respect, do not know in detail why.
Are we sufficiently informed as to the scope and limits of state planning? It is not enough to talk about emergencies without explaining them fully to the people. The question of communication is vitally important, because without public support for government policies the best-laid plans will fail. The Canadian people are not sufficiently informed of the intentions behind each aspect of government policy. Owing to this lack of general understanding, a whole series of questions is being asked throughout the country. The very variety of those questions points to the fact that the people do not see the end objectives of all this planning and regulation.
Many are disturbed in the first place, thinking that only lip service is given to responsible government. Some have even gone so far as to call it caucus or cabinet government. What guarantee is there that these emergency powers will not continue indefinitely? What of this creeping inflation which seems to be spreading, reducing the

The Budget-Mr. Macnaughton value of the dollar, slashing the value of accumulated savings, eating up the value of investments and discouraging personal savings and thrift? What of the mounting high cost of living, and the misery and hardship that result as a consequence? What of price control? What of the social services, old age pensions and security generally? What of the forty-plus age group, and those of sixty and over? What about the rights of labour under the new defence productive effort, and for that matter the rights of capital? Are the legitimate returns from efficient management and the investment of capital, which are so much needed for the expansion of our industry and development of our resources, to be denied? Surely we are now agreed that an excess profits tax, to quote the words of the Minister of Finance "blunts the edge of efficiency and invites waste."
What we are looking for is a way to tax excessive profits. But this whole matter has become so involved in misinformation it is almost an "excess-politics tax". What is to be the plight of that body of hardworking, intelligent, honest and generally thrifty people, caught between organized labour on one side and organized capital on the other side, and battered generally by a rising cost of living? Have we nothing to say to them? Have we no surcease to offer?
All of us in this House of Commons know that considerable thought is given to these problems. We know some of the answers. We know that a federal old age pension security scheme has been offered to the provinces, and is now under consideration by them. We know that the problem of small businessmen and the question of how small industry can be integrated in the over-all defence effort is receiving close attention. We know that procedure, looking to the channelling of defence production information to potential subcontractors, is being set up, and that the proper allocation of materials and military orders is being studied. We know that in the face of national danger the Canadian way is to gather round the government table and pool our ideas, resources and energies.
But do the people know this? Controls which are arbitrarily imposed and seem unreasonable meet public apathy and evasion. But if they are explained I submit the people will accept them with good grace. Even more, if Canadians are informed of the necessary objectives, they will themselves find ways in which to aid the government, and their initiative will often lead them to the objective faster than regulation can do it. This, then, is a plea for interpretation.


There is certainly one aspect of our national scene which, more than any other, needs interpretation at this moment. I refer to the high cost of living. It touches everyone. It concerns the people more than anything else. We are encountering a dangerous cycle of rising costs and rising prices. The housewife, who today has to spend 170 cents for what cost her 100 cents a few years ago, is obsessed with the difficulty of making ends meet on the average wage earner's income. One of the first things this government, and this whole parliament, might do is address itself to the defence of the buying power of the wage earner's dollar. Perhaps it is an exaggeration, but most of us will agree that we feel a fair wage today is twice what we are getting, and a fair price is half what we want to pay. Right or wrong, that is the way we secretly feel-that is all of us who have not the true facts by which to judge.
We know that taxes must be levied to maintain responsible government, and that taxes inevitably become interwoven in the price system. Possibly there is in the field of price determination some room for wider examination. The mark-up on sheer physical cost is one thing, but the mark-up on taxes included in the price structure savours of pyramiding and hence gouging the public. Thus, for example, if a new tax on a unit is one dollar, and if the mark-up on that dollar is another 35 cents, it savours of profiteering, pure and simple. I do not complain about the physical costs entering into an article, but I do think the government should step into the mark-up field and insist on fair play for producer and consumer.
We are all anxious to end this rising tide of prices, and it is the duty of the government to take whatever reasonable measures it can in an attempt to stabilize prices. It seems to me that, as a result of the Korean war, many prices have been deliberately increased in expectation of ultimate price control. This effort to establish a high price level is, to a considerable degree, responsible for rising costs. Unless this sort of thing can be avoided, price control may become a measure of last resort, and we shall bring on ourselves an economic strait-jacket. The Minister of Finance is entitled to our thanks for the sincere attempt which has been made to stop the rising cycle of prices. But if parliament cannot find something effective, then we are in for a great period of unrest.
In an issue as vital as inflation, policy must be right. But before we can halt the apparent deterioration of the purchasing power of the dollar in our pockets, we have to explain why it must be halted. Our failure to do so is perhaps the one really weak link in our

otherwise strong defence chain. I agree wholeheartedly with the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) when he said in this house, as reported at page 1762 of Hansard for April 9:
The greatest contribution any Canadian can make to stop inflation is to avoid panicky buying and to produce as much as possible. All of us should be thinking in terms of working harder; of working longer hours, rather than shorter hours. There is too much of a tendency, it seems to me, for people to look to government for solutions to their problems. Governments can help and should help in dealing with inflation; but consumers, labour unions, farm organizations, and businessmen can do much by their own efforts to reduce the pressures that lead to higher prices.
Even the Montreal Gazette of Tuesday, April 17, in its leading editorial under the heading "Home-made Inflation" said in part:
But it is also true that a high percentage of inflation is home-made, and is very definitely a domestic product.
And it is largely a domestic product because Canadians seem to have made up their minds that they want more leisure for more money. Or if they do work longer hours, they expect a large premium for the effort.
It might seem strange that this young country, reputed to be so full of vigour, should see fit to choose this leisurely way of living, for which so large a price must be paid in the depreciation of money values. But there is a growing favour for the mistaken belief that it is still possible to earn more without producing more.
Farther down the article reads:
As Mr. Abbott pointed out in his budget address: "If we are to carry greatly increased defence costs without having a definite fall in our standards of consumption . . . we shall all have to work harder and longer."
In plain terms, Mr. Speaker, the national pie is only so big. If one pressure group succeeds in carving out for itself a larger piece than it is entitled to, then the rest of us will suffer. That is what has been happening to us, and the only way for us to get out of the mess is for all of us to concentrate on increasing the size of the pie so that we all get a bigger piece. The need for hard work and the importance of curbing our appetites must be continually reiterated if we are to lick inflation.
When orders such as "credit restrictions" and others of like nature are made, whether as a result of suggestions from the Department of Finance, the Bank of Canada or otherwise, then it becomes the obligation of the government to explain them and to see to it that the explanation is understood, right down to the grass roots of the nation.
Most people are having considerable difficulty in understanding just what credit regulations mean; and I maintain that if the government wants the co-operation of all the sensible Canadians in this country, then they must go out and explain down to the last 80709-149
The Budget-Mr. Macnaughton detail, and give the very good reasons, the high purposes and serious objectives which induced credit restriction.
It is not good enough for some bureaucrat to wave a wand in Ottawa and expect that Miss Millennium will arrive on the next train from Utopia. To succeed, government policy must have the full co-operation of the people; but that co-operation will not be forthcoming until the people fully understand what is the end objective of that policy. In fact, it is the government's duty to the nation to make sure that all policies are fully understood-not only those in such vital issues as inflation, but those in all matters affecting parliament and the public. None of this is to say that the government is not doing a great deal better in this regard than many other governments. Such comments as I have made are in the hope only of further improving our lines of communication.
Today the government not only has the duty of formulating policy and seeing that it is carried out by an efficient bureaucracy, but the results of its own bureaux of research and investigation must also be made public and brought to the attention of the citizens at large. Hence, there is a great need, in fact an obligation, on the part of this or any other Canadian government to supply factual, unbiased and non-partisan information. Anything which lessens the vitality of this essential communication between the people and the government would appear to be opposed to the public interest.
This house will be disposed to give credit where it is due to the ministers for their comprehensive statements on broad policy. Yet if there is still such uneasiness in the country, further remedy must be sought. The place of parliament in the lines of communication between government and country is recognized; and it need not be emphasized here, of all places, that it is in part through hon. members themselves, in their addresses and personal meetings in their constituencies, that government policy reaches the grass roots. Accordingly, we receive a great deal of information; our desks groan under the deluge of reports and schemes. If we had more leisure most of us could boil down the spate of information on government activity and policy and use it to show our constituents just what the policy of the government was intended to be.
But lacking leisure, we need summaries and analyses; we need brief human statements of the intentions behind such and such a measure, couched in terms of the individual; then we in turn can go to our constituents. It is here, I think, that some criticism may be levelled against government
2328	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Macnaughton departments, bearing in mind always that the capacity to make a succinct human statement is a gift capriciously bestowed or laboriously learned. It is lucidity we want today, not diffused brilliance. Given the tools of communications, most of us would use them effectively.
Now let us glance at other channels of communication open to the government; and a study should be made of whether they are being enlisted to the best advantage of the nation. As everybody knows, these channels are the daily, the periodical and the weekly press, the radio, eventually television, moving pictures, the advertising industries and also the publishing industry. Who will deny that these avenues for information are the largest and most effective in the country? It is most important that government information should always be available to these great groups.
First, of course, is the press. Here our prime contact is with the press gallery. This house and the gallery are like next door neighbours. We know a great deal about each other, and a common prudence sometimes checks our tongues. It is not very often that we here acknowledge the essential function of the press gallery in our system of government. All in all, the sense of responsibility of gallery correspondents is very high. While they may be hired in a private interest, they traditionally and rightly look upon themselves as servants of the public interest.
Meantime, all is not well so far as the volume of information emanating from Ottawa is concerned. The press relies much upon the big wire services. I am told that Canada's main news services have been forced to make adjustments which appear, at first sight at any rate, to amount to drastic curtailment. Thus, at a time of world crisis, the average Ottawa news coverage by the leading agency has been reduced from 8,000 words daily to 4,000, and the United Kingdom bureau has been sharply depleted. I cannot help but feel that the United Nations and Washington should have more full-time press representatives from Canada. The present number is incredibly small.
Do the hon. members in this house, or do the people, know that the estimated cost to Canada of participation in the "United Nations and specialized agencies" for the fiscal year 1950-51 will amount to more than $15 million? If we are justified in spending this amount of money, is it not important that the people should know what their representatives are saying and doing? How can we hope to have public support for Canadian foreign policy when we are not getting a balanced report, as seen through Canadian


eyes, and prepared especially for Canadian consumption? As so many of the problems of Canada come from our efforts to meet a menacing international situation, international news, reported by Canadians for Canadian consumption, is very much our concern.
At a time when world affairs are in such a jittery state I would have thought it essential that the United Kingdom, the centre of commonwealth activities, Washington, the centre of North American and Pacific activities, and Lake Success, the centre of world activities, should have a great many more accredited Canadian correspondents reporting the news for the Canadian public. There are one or two outstanding exceptions to this general statement. The job being done by the correspondent of the Montreal Star at Lake Success proves what could and should be done.
It is encouraging to see that, although news coverage has fallen off badly in spots, the news coverage of the C.B.C. continues to hold its high standard and C.B.C. foreign representation appears to be healthily on the increase. The great success of the domestic Monday night C.B.C. program, where the correspondents quiz the ministers, is further evidence of the general public's need for information on, and its avid interest in, how the affairs of this country are being run and why.
In passing, a compliment is due also to another official agency partially in the news field. I refer to the reconstituted national film board. This board, by the high acceptability of its films and by the large number of its outlets, is doing a national communication service worthy of recognition. But I wonder how many know that the film board's movies are seen regularly in some 3,300 Canadian communities. Film board men are bringing useful films, information and advice on using them to workers in every field of Canadian life.
Another important medium of communication is the field of public relations. Are we doing a job in this field? No one will accuse the Department of National Health and Welfare of hiding its light under a bushel, nor should they do so because their work is both instructional and educational. But how many persons realize that in the last two years, through the initiative of the department, the federal government has been responsible for the construction of 27,000 new hospital beds, many of them in my own constituency, in a total of 40,000? I doubt if the people of this country realize the revolution which has been brought about, nationally speaking, in national health and public welfare owing to the initiative and research policies of the department.

Will anyone deny that the Department of National Revenue is certainly in need of public relations men to explain why the painful process of collecting taxes is so necessary to the just operation of our system?
Let me give you another illustration. I doubt very much whether the people of Montreal and district know how much the federal government, acting through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has done to assist housing in the greater Montreal area. I have been a constant critic of this corporation. I think its powers are too large and I think it should be brought under closer parliamentary supervision. But in fairness I must say that, upon inquiry, I find that "in the three years 1948-49-50 a total of
38.600	new housing units were completed in Montreal. Of this total, 14,500 were built with government assistance under the terms of the National Housing Act while another
1.600	units were built on direct government account for rental to veterans. Therefore over 42 per cent of all new housing units completed in Montreal in the past three years were constructed with government financial assistance or were built on direct government account."
"In dollar value the total amount of loans approved for Montreal under the National Housing Act in the past three years was $130 million while the total for the province of Quebec was $163 million. Direct government expenditure on new housing for veterans in the same period in Montreal totals $9 million."
And so it goes. The illustrations are legion and the wealth of information which should be brought to the attention of the citizens of Canada is almost comparable to the iron ore deposits in Labrador or the copper and silver deposits in the Yukon. All these little items of so-called local concern, small in themselves, but joined together, go to show the people of Canada that their money is being well spent. They create a feeling of justice and fair play and belief in our system of government. They prove that our government is not some colossus remote from the people, but is a collection of devoted, hard-working individuals, trying to do their best for the country.
One huge information service is to be avoided in the interest of an efficient operation. Inevitably it would become a natural target for partisan political attack and would be forced to operate constantly in a non-stable climate. I believe that the departments themselves should retain their information services in the interest of maximum efficiency. What we need is a traffic manager as it were, somebody to sift the available information 80709-149J
24. 1951
The Budget-Mr. Macnaughton and arrange for it to be disseminated, someone who would be responsible directly to the cabinet. He should have a small staff of recognized competence and the salaries scale available to his office should be such as to make this possible.
His functions and responsibility under the cabinet would be, first, to review all statements on a national policy level, thus making possible the uniform expression through a variety of spokesmen. This is the highest level of federal information.	Second, he
should counsel and guide the various departments and agencies on information policies, techniques and needs. Third, he should have an over-all responsibility to investigate and suggest the elimination of duplication in the various information services.	He should
conduct an annual survey of these operations and require periodic reports from them. Fourth, he should provide liaison with the several communication groups. An important function would be to sound out, seek and secure the active co-operation of existing private agencies, and in so far as possible, without government expense. Most of us recall the great service rendered to this nation during the war by private associations, professional groups and industry and it is reasonable to assume that they would co-operate fully in current non-partisan information programs for the general benefit of the nation. In this way also, we would avoid duplicating functions already performed by existing private organizations. Fifth, he should make public a yearly review of the information service as an additional aid and safeguard. Our traffic manager might be assisted by a non-partisan public relations advisory group chosen from recognized leaders in the field to serve without remuneration and to be available to the information manager for professional counsel. This suggestion is primarily a managing device to supply some measure of order in the present information service chaos and to establish standards of efficiency and economy.
Statements of national policy should be cleared through the office of our traffic manager but functional operations should remain in the departments where they can be most efficient. Under the general guidance of our traffic manager each department under the authority of its chief should undertake a survey of present information functions and practices with the purpose of eliminating waste, overlapping, duplication of activities, unnecessary publications and press releases. For the test should be public need. Once the basic survey has been made it should be kept current by less extensive surveys on a yearly basis.

The Budget-Mr. Green
Extraordinary efforts are made by the great corporations of Canada to keep the public informed of their activities and to be prepared to answer questions. The government of the country is by far the greatest business in it. Judged by the public relations efforts of big business the government lags behind. Clearly the government must not use the taxpayer's money to do propaganda for itself and try to perpetuate itself in office, but it is entitled to say what it is trying to do. Indeed, I contend that it fails in its duty if it does not.
