speechtext:
To come to my own views on budget policy, may I say that there are, in my opinion, and I think the opinion will be shared by most members in the house today, two vital problems facing the Canadian people and the Canadian parliament in this year, 1951. The first problem is preventing a third world war, and the second is halting the rise in the cost of living and preventing runaway inflation.
The budget must be considered in the light of its effect on these two great problems. In a free country perhaps the must effective way a government can deal with any problem is by framing budget policy to meet that particular problem. So today let us consider whether the Canadian Minister of Finance in 1951 has submitted to parliament a budget plan which meets these two problems as directly and as effectively as they could be met. To put it in another way, is the Canadian government giving leadership, or is its policy one of drift at a time when leadership is needed as never before?
To deal first with the question of the budget and the problem of preventing a third world war, it is true that the minister's budget provides a very large sum for defence expenditures. The figure will be found at

page 1806 of Hansard, and it is $1,664 million out of an estimated expenditure for the fiscal year from April 1, 1951, to March 31, 1952, of approximately $3,700 million. This expenditure for defence purposes is an increase of $893 million over similar expenditures in the fiscal year which has just ended, but of course a portion of that increase is caused by the rising prices. But I should like to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members, the minister's own summary of budget policy, as it is set out at page 1807 of Hansard. This is the key, in my opinion, to his whole budget policy for this year, where he says:
I am reluctant to believe that we must inevitably face budgets of $4 billion or more for any considerable succession of years. There is still a possibility that reasonable solutions of the present international tensions may be developed. In another year's time we should have a clear view of the prospects. I have, therefore, decided not to recommend any major reconstruction of our tax system this year but instead to meet our current requirements by a series of simple but adequate surcharges on several existing taxes and also to widen the coverage of our special excise taxes. I think that over the shorter run-
And those are significant words, "the shorter run".
-this method of defence surcharges will produce the necessary revenue with the least difficulty and inconvenience.
Those words, too, are significant-"with the least difficulty and inconvenience".
If our optimistic hopes are realized it will be easy to reduce these surcharges or to drop them entirely, but I want to add that if it becomes clear that we are in for a long pull at these high levels of expenditure some major changes in the existing tax structure may have to be devised. My tax proposals, therefore, must be regarded as an interim policy for the period of the current year.
That paragraph merits careful analysis. It implies that the problem of preventing a third world war may vanish overnight. It also implies that international tension may be solved at any time, certainly during the coming fiscal year. Unfortunately there is nothing whatever to justify this attitude. I wish with all my heart that there were, but there is absolutely nothing in the world situation today to justify that attitude by the Canadian Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). He is lulling the people of Canada to sleep; he is soothing them at a time when they should be aroused.
Furthermore the statements in this paragraph contain the admission that there is need for major changes in the tax structure of Canada, if we are in for a long pull. This forces us to consider whether or not we are in for a long pull. The minister has decided we are not, and he adopts deliberately a short-run plan. What is

that plan? In effect it is to get the extra money with the least difficulty and inconvenience, not to the taxpayer but to the tax collector. The main way of getting it is by a surcharge on existing taxes, and widening the coverage of certain excise taxes. This 1951 budget is a tax collector's budget.
A further implication from the minister's speech is that a year from now perhaps- and there is nothing definite about it- Canadians will get a long-term budget policy which, I submit, is what they should have had this year. Here, clearly, is a policy of drift, not of leadership. Here we have a complete failure to realize the situation of Canada and her allies.
You see, Mr. Speaker, the policy of the free nations of the world today is quickly to become so strong that the Soviets dare not start a third world war. The policy is not only to become strong quickly, but also to continue strong until Russia decides that it is in her interests to co-operate.
Every party in the house approves of this policy. I believe every party in Canada, except the communist party, approves of it: it is the Canadian policy. It is new for us, just as it is new for the Americans. Our experience in two world wars was that we were thrown into them practically overnight, and concentrated all our energies on winning. Then when peace came, when the fighting stopped, we disbanded our forces and returned to our civilian occupations just as quickly as possible.
Today we are faced with an entirely different problem which is that, while at peace, we must become strong enough to win a war, and must continue in that condition. I believe the policy Canada and other free nations have embarked upon is a very difficult one, more difficult even than a full-out war policy. It is perfectly clear we must be strong and prepared all the time until the policy of the free nations succeeds. And remember, if and when that policy fails, we are right in the middle of a third world war.
Obviously this is not a short-run policy; it is a long-term policy. It cannot possibly succeed in one year or in two years. Even if the war in Korea were to end tomorrow- and we know how little likelihood there is of its ending for a long time, in the light of press dispatches of the last day or two- that would not finish the policy of being strong. The defence expenditures would still go on; we would still have to be prepared to defend our way of life.
The war in Korea is merely one attempt to prevent a third world war. Even when
The Budget-Mr. Green the war in Korea is won, that does not terminate the need for the policy of being strong. I hold in my hand the report of a question and answer interview of General George C. Marshall, Secretary of Defense of the United States. This appears in U.S. News and World Report for April 13, 1951. Incidentally I would point out that General Marshall is one of the greatest leaders of our generation; I do not believe his wisdom can be questioned by anyone. In this article, which bears the heading "Prepare For Ten Years of Tension", General Marshall was asked many questions, of which I shall quote only one:
Question: Do you consider, then, that what people have got to do is to bear in mind the over-all picture constantly instead of some little lessening of tension in Korea or perhaps some other part of the world?
Answer:	Put it this way; the best we can hope
for, as I see it, is a prolonged tension rather than an all-out war. What we hope and pray for at the present time is that, as between the two, it might be a prolonged tension rather than war, during which we can build up our strength and our resources, get organized in western Europe, which General Eisenhower, supreme commander in Europe, is trying to do-get straightened out, we hope, in the Far East-but that's the best hope at present. If we should get a complete agreement with the Soviets we would be perfect fools to relax our military strength until we had evidence of good faith.
Unfortunately, the tendency already is to relax.
The reference there is to the United States.
That's what we have to fight against.
Further on he states that he believes the free nations are in for a period of ten years of tension. Canadians were entitled to have a long-term budget policy, but instead they have been told by the Minister of Finance to wait a year. That is bound to bewilder them and cause apathy; it is bound to bring about a failure to realize that the problem of preventing a third world war is a long-term one.
We have here once more a policy of drift and indecision, just as we have a policy of drift and indecision about raising a force for Europe. In the speech from the throne we found these words:
Progress has been made in the organization of an integrated force in Europe under the North Atlantic treaty organization. The supreme commander. General Eisenhower, has recently visited Canada to consult with the government and the chiefs of staff. You will be asked early in the session to authorize Canadian participation in this integrated force as part of our program for national defence and security.
The session has now been going on for practically three months but we have not yet had any statement as to when this force is to be sent to Europe. There are no troops available to send. It is perfectly clear that the men who were raised for the special force

The Budget-Mr. Green will be needed to reinforce the brigade which has gone to Korea. The preparation of forces for Europe will take months. Yet the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said that 1951 is the dangerous year; that this is the year in which we must make a great effort if we are to prevent a third world war.
There is also drift and indecision about establishing an effective reserve army. We rely in Canada for defence from hostile aircraft on reserve anti-aircraft units. The city of Ottawa depends upon a reserve unit to defend it from hostile air attacks, as does my home city of Vancouver. In both cases those units have iust skeleton forces, totally and completely unable to defend their respective cities. If we are to raise any large numbers of troops we must do it by means of the reserve army. Although this session has gone on for three months we have had no statement yet from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) as to how he proposes to raise a reserve army. He carefully refrained from dealing with that subject when he spoke earlier in the session and nothing has been said about it since by him.
We have a policy of drift and indecision too in connection with Canada taking part in a Pacific defence pact. The other day the President of the United States announced that there was to be a Pacific pact between the United States, Australia and New Zealand. When we questioned the minister of external affairs about Canada's part he said that the pact was only for the western Pacific. Apparently the government is not interested in such a plan.
Let me point out that if this policy of being strong is to succeed it must be extended to cover the Pacific area as well as the Atlantic. There is not much use stopping a war in the Atlantic if a first-class war can break out in the Pacific. Although Canada is a nation on the Pacific and has several thousand troops now crossing that great ocean to take part in the Korean war, she is not participating in this new defence pact for the Pacific. I think it is a disgrace.
Furthermore, there are two other examples of drift and indecision on the part of this government, one being the failure to crack down on profiteering. Not one move has been made to check profiteering, and very little has been done to halt rising prices. These are just examples of the indecision and drift of the government. The fact of the matter is that this government is so firmly entrenched and has such a large and meek majority that the ministers have become smug and self-satisfied. They have neither the
(Mr. Green.]

will nor the vision to work out a long-term budget policy. So much for the budget and the prevention of a third world war.
I come now to my second question, that
is,	the cost of living and inflation. Certainly this is a vital problem. Since the outbreak of war in Korea Canadians have seen some interesting and disturbing things happen. First of all, they have seen prices and the cost of living rise steadily. I have here a clipping which sums up these increasing prices very neatly. It is a dispatch from Edmonton dated April 10 and quotes Hon. W. C. Woodward, a former lieutenant governor of British Columbia, who I think is as good a merchant as this country ever produced. This reads:
Woodward (Yes) Urges Stop Buying
Edmonton, April 10-(CP)-The way to bring prices down is for people to stop buying, Honourable W. C. Woodward of Vancouver, president of Woodward Stores Limited, said Monday in an interview.
"That may be a surprising statement for a merchant but that's the way I feel about it. There is no reason for these high prices."
Canadians have seen their government threatening to put on controls, but not doing
it.	Surely the government either should have put on controls at once or made a definite statement that there were to be no controls. Instead they said that they would not put them on now but might put them on a little later if the people were not good. The result was that right down the line from the manufacturer to the retailer prices have gone up in an effort to be prepared for the time controls are brought in. There has been unfair profit making across this country since the outbreak of war in Korea. Just two weeks ago a Gallup poll was held in which this question was asked: Do you think there is much profiteering (unfair profit making) going on in Canada now? Three out of every four persons who answered that question said that they thought the Canadian people were the victims of unfair profiteering. I think it could be more fairly described as unfair profit making. There is no doubt that that has been going on and unfortunately the ministry must accept a large share of the blame for what has happened because of their indecision in dealing with the question of controls.
There are other startling things the Canadian people have seen in this intervening period. They have seen the value of their government bonds drop below par although it was understood throughout the country that that would never be allowed to happen. They have seen the value of their savings and their insurance cut drastically. Pensioners of all kinds are being squeezed, unions are being forced to demand increased wages, and

white-collar workers once again are trapped and helpless to meet the situation. It seems to me that there has been an utter failure on the part of the members of the Canadian cabinet to realize the tragic suffering there has been throughout the country. Private members of the Liberal party realize that condition because we have heard them raise it on the floor of the house time and again, but I do not believe that members of the cabinet yet realize the suffering there has been, and which is still going on today.
We were told that the budget would meet the problem of the increasing cost of living and inflation. Everyone expected budget measures designed for this purpose. Instead what have we got? We have a slapping on of extra taxes of the type which are most easily collected, obviously with no definite policy in mind to halt the rise in the cost of living or to prevent the spread of inflation. In fact in some ways the budget is actually forcing the spread of inflation, throwing oil on a fire which is already burning much too briskly in Canada.
I have several criticisms to make of the budget. First of all may I refer to the increase in the sales tax from 8 per cent to 10 per cent which is an increase of 25 per cent in the tax itself. As hon. members know, the sales tax is imposed at the manufacturer's level. It pyramids of course. At each turnover there is a profit mark-up, and that mark-up includes a mark-up on the tax. It hits the poor harder than the rich. The sales tax takes no account of ability to pay. There is no exemption for lower incomes as in the case of the income tax. It is bound to increase the cost of living, and it is directly inflationary. I have very good authority for the statement that the sales tax is inflationary, no less an authority than the Minister of Finance himself. When he delivered his baby budget speech on September 7 of last year he said, as reported at page 423 of Hansard:
In selecting the particular measures to recommend to the house we have tried to take no action that would cause any significant increase in the costs of the day-to-day essential items of consumer expenditure. For this reason I do not propose any change in either the rate or the application of the general sales tax . . .
He did go on to say that the sales tax was not as bad as it was pictured, but there was his definite policy just six or seven months ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That has nothing to do with inflation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us read again what he said. It is as follows:
In selecting the particular measures to recommend to the house we have tried to take no action that
The Budget-Mr. Green would cause any significant increase in the costs of the day-to-day essential items of consumer expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What has that to do with inflation?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has a great deal. It is because of the increasing prices that we are getting inflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is confusing cause and effect.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister is confusing the hard time the people are having with government policy. Today there is amazement across the country at the reversal of the attitude of the Minister of Finance in the short period of six months. I believe that the criticism of the increase in the sales tax is universal; it is in practically every leading paper in Canada regardless of political allegiance. I suggest to the minister that it is not yet too late to drop the increase in the sales tax. To do so would probably start a movement of prices downward. Nothing would do more to raise the morale of the Canadian people, and their attitude is of the first importance in fighting the battle against inflation. Probably there is nothing the government could do which would go farther toward solving the problem than to change its mind and cut out the increase in the sales tax.
I realize that the result would be a loss of $105 million estimated revenue for the present fiscal year, but the minister is budgeting for a surplus of $30 million. Government revenues are buoyant and will continue so because defence preparations are bound to continue. The minister has consistently underestimated his surpluses. In the baby budget speech of September of last year, when he had only six months of the year left, he estimated a surplus of $15 million. As things turned out, he had a surplus of $203 million, almost thirteen times the amount of his estimate. He certainly is not a very good estimator. There is no need for a surplus under present conditions.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Probably he does it deliberately.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) says, it may be that he does this pessimistic estimating deliberately.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, that is not true.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He cannot figure figures.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps he cannot figure. That may be the answer.

The Budget-Mr. Green

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That may be the answer, yes. I have always felt that prophecy was diffioolt.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If it turns out that there is a
prospect of a deficit of $75 million or a lesser sum, then expenditures can be cut further than contemplated during the present year. I cannot think of a stronger incentive for saving by the government.
The question of saving brings me to my next criticism of the minister'si taxation policy. There is absolutely no incentive in the budget to the individual to save, and savings by Canadians could do a great deal to halt price increases and prevent inflation. The fact is that people have simply been unable to save because of rising prices. When the minister dealt with that question, as reported at page 1799 of Hansard, he did a bit of whining. He said:
Personal spending increased more than personal incomes, resulting in a decline in net personal savings out of current income. This decline in new savings amounted to about $270 million, or a drop of about 30 per cent.
Then he went on to point out the need for saving. He made a great plea to the Canadian people to do more saving. Where they were to get the money for saving he did not explain. At page 1803 we find these words:
There is also urgent need for a higher volume of new saving, to cover the increase in capital investment which is in prospect, and to restrain the rising trend in consumer spending. This is certainly one of the best ways of reducing the intensity of competition for the use of labour and materials, and so reducing the upward pressure on prices.
Then he went on to say:
The money saved can be used to buy Canada savings bonds, or to pay off the mortgage on his house or farm more rapidly, or to speed up the repayment of other debts, or to increase his savings in any other form that suits his individual circumstances. The important thing is to achieve an increase in aggregate savings up to a level at least equal to the new capital investment which we shall have to make this year.
One would have thought there would be contained in the budget policy some incentive to the people to save, but there is nothing whatever. In fact, the budget makes savings practically impossible. Mr. Speaker, inflationary conditions abroad in the world today call for a reward for saving. I thought the position was made very clear by Mr. James Muir, the president of the Royal Bank, in his annual statement to the shareholders in January of this year. Mr. Muir is quoted as saying:
The most powerful weapon in the fight against inflation is generally supposed to be a stiff increase in the income tax. But the test of efficiency must be that any income tax increases shall penalize spending and reward saving.

He explains that further by saying:
. . . equity and efficiency alike demand the exemption from income tax, wherever possible, of the bona fide saving of the public. In its simplest form, this might include the limited exemption of insurance premiums and of net purchases of savings bonds over the year.
With inflationary conditions today, increased insurance is a necessity for all family men. Mortgage payments have been assumed by our young couples that would have terrified my generation. When we see them taking on mortgages of $8,000 or $10,000, all these tremendously high figures, we wonder how on earth they are ever going to be able to pay them off. The time has come when there should be some budget policy designed to reward these young couples, and anyone else, who will save for purposes such as paying off a mortgage or purchasing a reasonable amount of insurance. This is one instance where a long-term budget policy would have been of great benefit.
My third criticism of taxation policy is directed against the levying of the 15 per cent excise tax on necessities, particularly stoves and washing machines. The tax is not being imposed on stoves using wood or coal. If a person happens to use electricity, gas, or oil for cooking, then the tax is payable on a stove of that type. I think it would have been wiser for the minister to exempt stoves of all kinds up to a certain value. Then, if people wanted to buy more expensive stoves, let them pay the excise tax. You see, you cannot turn the clock back and force everyone to use a coal or wood stove. I am told that in greater Vancouver there are over 86,000 homes using gas, electricity or oil, and 40,000 using all other kinds of fuel. To put a tax on these electric, oil and gas stoves as well as ordinary washing machines is merely increasing the cost of living. I believe that should not have been done.
This brings me to the fourth point. The minister could have made up any loss by increasing the tax on liquor. There has been no increase in the tax on liquor, although everyone in the country who drinks expected -I do not happen to be one of those people, but certainly all my drinking associates in the house expected-that there would be an increase in the tax on liquor. There would have been very little protest. The minister gives as his reason that liquor is already highly taxed. He proceeded to tax cigarettes and tobacco to the tune of $35 million a year. It is amusing to read his statement of last year in introducing the baby budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Have you any vices that we could tax?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't answer, or they will do it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am afraid that the government can tax anything, so I am not going to answer that question. The minister's statement regarding liquor and tobacco taxes last September 7, is found at page 423 of Hansard. He said he was increasing the tax on liquor last September, and then went on to say:
I am not proposing any changes in tobacco taxes, which are already very high.
So we had the same reason last year about tobacco that we are getting now about liquor. I thought last year that he was bringing the liquor tax up to the level of the tobacco tax. Liquor certainly should have been hit in this present budget before cigarettes and tobacco, but instead liquor has been protected. Unfortunately, that leads to talk across the country that the liquor interests have the ear of the government, and rumours of this sort. It is a bad thing to get opinions of that sort abroad.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sure the public do not believe that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister might be surprised how many of the public do believe it. The minister made a great mistake in not increasing the tax on liquor.
Finally, on this problem of the cost of living and inflation, I believe that the house and the Canadian people should protest the proposal of the government to amend the British North America Act so that the provinces can levy an indirect tax on sales up to three per cent. That proposal has been set out, of course, in the appendices to Hansard. This would enable the provinces not only to levy direct taxes, as they can do at the present time, but also to levy indirect taxes. This is the price the provinces are demanding for paying 50 per cent of the old age pension of $40 per month for the aged from sixty-five to sixty-nine inclusive. What will that tax mean? It is certain to force prices up, certain to spread inflation. It will make it that much harder for our senior citizens to live. I do not know how they get along now on $40 per month. The real need today is for an increase in that basic payment of $40.
The provinces are not directly concerned with the fight against inflation. They are not very likely to worry a great deal about inflation. I am sure the minister has found that because he complained about them at page 1803 of Hansard, of April 10, 1951, and pointed out how much expenditures by 80709-150
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot provincial governments had been increased. He went on to say this:
Having regard to the impact of defence on construction materials and skills I must again urge the provinces and municipalities to review particularly their capital and construction programs in the light of the general public interest.
This is to be a hidden tax. The provinces will not have to disclose it to the people who buy. Of course, that is the very worst kind of tax possible. It certainly will not bring down the cost of living or curb inflation. I suggest that it would be far better for the dominion to set up a contributory pension scheme under which Canadians would pay as they earn, and then draw benefits as of right at sixty-five without a means test, and let the provinces add to the figure if they wish to do so.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that there is little that is inspiring in the budget policy. Once again the government has lost an opportunity to give leadership to the Canadian people-to give them a clear view either of the challenge which faces Canada or of the ways to meet that challenge successfully. Yet all the time the communists drive on relentlessly toward their goal of world domination. They are not working on any year-to-year basis. I suggest that the government should realize, before it is too late, that these two terrible problems which are faced by the Canadian people and, of course, by the Canadian parliament, can only be solved by aggressive leadership.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to speak following the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I have known him for a long time. He is one of the popular members of the house. He always prepares his speeches with great care. By the way, may I say that he was one of the members of the civil service committee some years ago, when I came to know him well. Since then we have been good friends.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We had a happy time on that committee.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We had a great time together. My hon. friend was one of the most helpful members of the committee.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, that I am obliged to disagree to a certain extent with my hon. friend. He spoke about young couples who assumed mortgages amounting to $8,000 or $10,000, and he said that they must have great confidence in the future. Indeed, they must; and they are right to be confident in th,e future. Probably the reason why they assumed such heavy responsibilities is that
233$

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot they had never heard any of the depressing speeches made by my hon. friend. If they had, they would not assume such responsibilities in connection with a home.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They would not get married.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps not. Perhaps if they took my hon. friend seriously, they would wait a long time before saying the final "yes". I am fond of the hon. gentleman; but as we are in an era of fundamental freedoms, when the fundamental freedoms or human rights are talked about so much, we may differ. He spoke of the policy of drift and indecision followed by the government and quoted a speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) last year. He referred to some statements that were made by him at the time. Until then the policy of the government had been different, and the government had not embarked upon a three-year policy for spending $5 billion for defence preparations. I am sure that policy was undertaken partly on the advice of my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra contained in the forceful speech he made last June in answer to mine with regard to the Korean affair. When 1 protested against the expedition to Korea, I remember that my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and a new member from Quebec said that I was all wrong, that we should defeat the communists on their own territory in Korea, that Canada should send a large expedition there and that we should have armies in all parts of the world. That has been the policy of the hon. gentleman for a long time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend is stretching that quite far.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No. Even today my hon. friend complained that the expeditionary force to Europe is not ready, although thousands of our boys have been sent to Korea. I prefer what was said the other day by the financial critic of the opposition, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). I heard him well, and I was satisfied to hear him express such a view as the one he then expressed, not because he repeated what I had said but because he showed some courage in saying it. He said that it was the view of many people in Toronto that the troops we have in Korea should be brought back to this country. But I will not pursue the matter further. I will however tell my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that from the start he has been speaking like General Crerar and General MacArthur.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am in good company.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When they hear of war, these gentlemen are like hounds at hunting time and they think of pursuing the enemy. I think a great deal of hounds; some of them are splendid and are extremely helpful in hunting game. But in this instance I say to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra- and I say the same thing to my other gifted friend, the hon. member for Lake Centre- that in the language he used in the house he has spoken like General Crerar and General MacArthur: We must defeat the enemy at all costs. It costs money. Here you are. You cannot complain about it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It costs a great deal more if the enemy defeats us.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps. But I do not speak of the budget of China or that of Korea. I speak of the budget of Canada. Both my friend the hon. member for Quadra and the hon. member for Lake Centre, and some others on the other side of the house, have been insistently declaring that we were not doing enough, that we should do more and more; and here we are. We are spending more money, and that money must come from the pocket of the Canadian taxpayer. The result cannot be otherwise. The last men who can be heard to complain about the increase in taxation are my hon. friend and all those who have insisted on these military achievements. I am not a pacifist; but at the time this policy was embarked on I was afraid of precisely what my hon. friend is complaining of now; but he has been insisting on it all the time.
We have a North Atlantic pact. He must be satisfied with it inasmuch as he did not say much about it, except that we are not fulfilling our duty, that we are not sending troops now to Europe under General Eisenhower. This is what he said, and I heard him very well. He accused the government of following a policy of drift and indecision because they have not enough men to send there. It costs money to send more men there. It may be in the three-year defence plan, but it will cost more money, and it will entail taxation. My hon. friend is too bright a lawyer and too able a politician not to realize that fact. He must be the first one to realize it. I would say that he and my other gifted friend, the hon. member for Lake Centre, must realize it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is in the defence expenditures.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, it is in the defence expenditures; but it can be done only at the proper time. If my hon. friend insists on doing more, the Canadian people will have to pay more,

and they will have to tighten their belts accordingly. My hon. friend knows it. I do not expect to convince him, because I know he is sincere and that he has very deep feelings about it, and I respect his views. Although I sincerely believe in the freedom of thought in this house about political problems, 1 have the right to disagree with it, and moreover I have the right to tell him that he is illogical, and that he should praise the government for taxing the Canadian people for the expenditure that he has been calling for. Instead of accusing the government of indecision and drift, telling them that they have not yet established a policy on that, he should say to the government: I congratulate you on defending this country, on sending troops to Korea, and I hope that you will soon send that expeditionary force to Europe. But I have never prepared the speeches of the hon. gentleman and I am sure that he will not use my suggestions for his next speech.
He spoke of the reserve army. We have a reserve army in this country. He complained that we have a small number of reserve aircraft and anti-aircraft reserves.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, April 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Robinson for the second reading of Bill No. 118, to incorporate Border Pipeline Corporation.

When I was making my introductory remarks at the time this bill was last before the house I said that we in this group were opposed to this bill particularly on two grounds: First, because it was intended that this pipe line would be built with private capital; and second, because, according to the information we had, this company does not intend to pursue an all-Canadian route from the commencement of the pipe line through to the coast before it comes to United States territory.
I had also brought the attention of the house to the fact that we did have some support from other quarters of the house, and that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), and the former member for Vancouver Centre, had shown an identity of purpose and interest in the principle of publicly-owned pipe lines.
Before proceeding I should like to quote from the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), particularly as I see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) is in his seat at the present time. At page 2808 of Hansard for April 30, 1949, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni had this to say:
There is a very important principle involved. Last night I was protesting against what appeared to me to be a tremendous lack of vision on the part of the directors of our Canadian National Railways. That railway system is in the business of providing transportation and moving freight, whether it be in the form of coal, oil, gas or any other form.
The Canadian National directors are allowing this pipe line method of transportation to be laid all along their right of way. It will be in the hands of private corporations and this tremendous freight which is originating in this north country is going to provide corresponding profits. I sincerely hope that the volume of traffic will be such that the profits will be large.
I think the Canadian National directors-I would not say the Minister of Transport-have been remiss in their duties and have shown an appalling lack of vision in not having investigated this proposal very carefully. I for one, and I am sure this would apply to other hon. members, would have been glad to approve the capital required to put in these pipe lines which would have provided a tremendous amount of freight revenue.
I am tired of voting money to defray deficits. I should like to see the Canadian National look into this matter carefully before they permit private companies to lay transportation lines for gas and oil on their right of way. They and the Minister of Transport should look into the possibilities of this form of transportation being provided by the Canadian National system.
I am quite willing to follow the advice of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni in
Border Pipeline Corporation connection with a venture that presents opportunities for profit. I am quite sure if the hon. member for Comox-Alberni says that this is a profitable venture, there can be no question about it: it is a very profitable venture.
Then in the part of his speech I read he uses the expression "appalling lack of vision". Those are the words he used. They are strong words. If we understand correctly, the word "appalling" means horrible, and when coupled with the other words it would mean a horrible lack of vision, or a frightening lack of vision, or a terrible lack of vision, or a paralysing lack of vision. There, again, I think the words of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni can be accepted by all members in the house who are getting tired of seeing American capital come to Canada and pick the cream of Canadian investment and development.

While I was deeply interested in the fact that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni gave such strong support to the principle of public ownership of pipe lines, I was a little

Border Pipeline Corporation disappointed in another direction in the house. The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) has been an ardent fighter for an all-Canadian route. Everyone gives him credit for his off-the-cuff, his on-the-cuff and his in-the-cuff speeches. But, Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed in this respect that, after having the support of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, he does not come along with us and give us his support of the principle of public ownership of pipe lines.
I know he has thought about it. From his attitude on other questions which come before the house I know he has thought about it. He is a progressive friend of mine, and I would say that I am still hopeful. I believe the hon. member for Fraser Valley is just about to emerge from the cocoon of capitalist inhibition.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley has been greatly assisted by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott), who makes a rather dramatic approach at times when he talks on these questions.
Hear, hear.

I appreciate the blase
manner in which he can accept applause, without even turning a hair. I understand the hon. member for Springfield is now generally known throughout Manitoba as the Cruickshank of Manitoba. But we would like him to take another step, and not only support an all-Canadian route, but say that these pipe lines should be publicly owned, and that the profits from them should go to the Canadian people. We are not suggesting that that is socialism; it is a form of public ownership.
It is a service.

Yes, it is a service which should be given by the Canadian people to the Canadian people.
And I am pleased to note that the efforts of the small group in this corner of the chamber are having some effect. I remember when the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) used to sit at the other end of the chamber, and he voted time after time against public ownership. He was to be found with the private enterprisers. I have been informed -I am not quite sure about it, from personal experience-but I have been informed that recently in a committee which dealt with public ownership of pipe lines, and things of that kind, he has been putting forth some very strong arguments in that connection. I wish to mention in that respect that the hon. member for Kamloops has, since he voted against public ownership of pipe lines, moved down to this end of the chamber, and he now sits beside the hon. member for Cape Breton

South (Mr. Gillis). I am sure the personal contact and personal intimacy with and the fatherly advice he has received from the hon. member for Cape Breton South is having its influence. Next time this matter comes to a vote I expect to see him standing shoulder to shoulder with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.
We in this group stand for the principle of social ownership, generally. As hon. members know, our policy is based, in principle, on a program known as the Regina manifesto. In that program the third plank is known as social ownership, and deals with the necessity of social ownership of certain things in this country for the advantage of the Canadian people.
In agriculture?

Certainly not. I shall deal with that later. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) says "agriculture". Apparently he has not been reading the C.C.F. program, or he does not understand it, because he would not be saying that. I expect to hear later from the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) because I understand he has had a speech germinating for about six weeks.
We in this group believe that there is a place for a certain amount of planning in our economy. This idea was first put forward in 1932 and 1933 by the C.C.F. when it was first formed. At that time members of this party were looked upon with great disfavour, considerable misunderstanding and some horror by those who had nothing to do previously with the study of economics. But a wider and wider section of the Canadian people are beginning to realize just what we are advocating.
We submit that free enterprise, even under capitalism, has to be modified if the needs of the Canadian people are going to be met. That is obvious. How can we say that we are moving in a period of free enterprise when we see government, because of conditions and circumstances, more and more entering the field of public investment and so on? When you see the lordis of Bay street coming to Ottawa on their hands and knees, these tycoons of the gold mining industry, seeking aid and subsidies for the support of gold mines, we should remember they are the same people who reply to the ordinary working man who asks for a subsidy for bread and milk, "My dear fellow, you must stand on your own feet; you must earn' your own living." These things indicate the changing Canadian conditions. I am not opposed to subsidies for gold mines, I am simply pointing that out to illustrate that we are not in a totally free economy at this time.

There is no particular virtue in socialism for the sake of socialism. It is not because we have a doctrinaire conception that we advocate these things. We advocate them because we believe that if we are going to have a democratic and peaceful transition to a state of society with all possible advantages, when there will be returned to the great masses of workers and producers a just share of their production, it must be done by evolutionary and democratic methods, step by step, as a result of experience.
It was because of that belief that the Regina manifesto was drawn up and presented to the Canadian people as a program. These are policies that are in keeping with Canadian tradition, Canadian psychology and Canadian circumstances. I am relating what I say entirely to the question of public ownership of pipe lines.
We in this group believe generally that our next move in the economic field-in fact we believe we are moving into a mixed economy that contains certain types of ownership-is one that should consider public ownership first of all. In the federal field we propose public ownership of railways, water transport and, we hope, gas and oil pipe lines. In the provincial field we advocate public ownership of power production, public services and things of that type. In the municipal field there will be locally owned power plants and possibly public distribution of milk, bread and things of that sort.
What about eggs?

Easter has gone by and we have no eggs. We believe also in co-operative ownership at all levels. At the national level there would be co-operative marketing of the agricultural production of this country, credit unions, administrative and legislative organizations and things of that type. Then in the provincial field there would be co-operative organizations which would be closer to the people. At the local municipal level there would be the consumers' store, local farmers organizations and credit unions.
We believe that there is a field for considerable private ownership. If private ownership renders a service to the community without exploitation, without the improper development of natural resources, and without monopoly, we believe it can still perform a service for the country.
What about hardware?

Small hardware stores, not branch hardware stores. We are opposed to monopoly in all its phases when monopoly means operation without necessary control by the government, whether federal or provincial. Obviously we must have some form of
Border Pipeline Corporation monopoly. You cannot operate a vast telephone system efficiently without a certain amount of monopoly, and the same applies to other distributing agencies, such as those having to do with power and so on. We are not opposed to monopolies as a development within capitalism simply because they are monopolies. But we are opposed to monopolies because of their effect.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would appear the hon. member is going far afield.

I am simply illustrating the advantages of public ownership of pipe lines. If Your Honour will have patience for two of three minutes I think you will see I am quite in order. Every child in Canada is entitled to an education to the extent of his talents. Every adult is entitled to employment at satisfactory wages or salary throughout his working days. Every invalid is entitled to security. Every older person is entitled to a pension that will provide security with comfort.
We say that if a monopoly, whether it be a pipe line, a bus line, a mining monopoly or any type, is willing to operate or develop the natural resources of this country, conserving them under principles laid down by a government having the interests of the people at heart; if that monopoly is willing to pay a rate of taxation to provide a necessary standard of living and the things I have just mentioned; if that monopoly is willing to charge a fair price for its commodities or services: then we say that there is no particular virtue in socialization.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The principle of the bill concerns the construction of a pipe line.

There is no object in socialization for the sake of socialization, and if a monopoly is not able to meet these terms then we say it should be isocialized. I am sure that that would have the support of the great majority of the Canadian people if they were informed of the facts.
I shall deal now with the question of an all-Canadian route. Another objection we have to this bill is that the company will be made up largely of United States capital. I do not blame United States people for wanting to invest in pipe lines if they have the opportunity, because that might be a good thing to dio. In my opinion they cause considerable difference, and a different effect on the community and the economy. The investment of local capital means that you have people reinvesting their profits in the community, in the province or within Canada. They are taking an interest in the country. They have a personal stake in the country. They are living with the people who are

Border Pipeline Corporation working in their plants or factories, and these profits are reinvested from year to year in the country. So far as foreign investment is concerned, there is a complete loss to Canada of the total profits exported from this country each year from these operations.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian capital is preferable in all these ventures. We also believe that the people with capital in Canada have been very shortsighted in allowing outside capital to come in and take advantage of the opportunities to make these developments. As I said before, the reinvestment of profits from Canadian capital in the Canadian economy simply means that, while we may disagree as to the justice or adequacy of the distribution of the production of the company, there is no loss to Canada as a whole. The total wealth produced remains within Canada.
Our second major objection is that this company does not intend to build an allCanadian route. This matter concerns many people in British Columbia. The legislature of British Columbia has expressed itself in favour of an all-Canadian route, and so have farmers organizations and boards of trade. If I had the time I could have quoted this evening, from the Nelson Daily News published in my own district, a report of the meeting of the associated boards of trade of eastern British Columbia at which the delegates expressed great concern over the fact that gas or oil may be piped to the United States prior to reaching the Canadian coast. I could also quote the Ottawa Citizen and other papers but time does not permit me to do so this evening.
There is no question as to the value of these developments to Canada. Their value is recognized so far as the power possibilities are concerned, so far as employment is concerned, and their great value so far as revenue is concerned. There is no question that a route through the Kettle valley is feasible. We were told the greatest lot of boloney on a previous bill. We realize now that it was boloney. Prominent engineers questioned the feasibility of the route because of sliding ground and so on and made the whole thing appear almost impossible to us. As a result of cross-examining the engineers who are going to build! the Trans Mountain pipe line we know that from their point of view the Kettle valley route is an easy one, and presents no construction difficulties.
Therefore there is no argument whatever either from the financial or from the physical point of view against the building of a gas or oil pipe line from its source straight through the Kettle valley to Vancouver prior to entering the United States. We feel very

strongly about this matter, and I wish to move, seconded' by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones):
That Bill No. 118 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house further consideration of this bill should be deferred until the house has been assured that the route of any pipe line built by the proposed company will be laid out so as to serve Canadian requirements before any such pipe line leaves Canadian soil.
In view of certain remarks made by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham), I want to draw to the attention of the house the opinion of the Liberal members of the legislative assembly of Alberta with respect to the export of gas from that province. I should like to quote briefly from a Canadian Press dispatch of April 3 found in the Nelson Daily News for April 4. It reads in part as follows:
The bill permitting temporary export of natural gas to Montana for essential defence production yesterday received second reading in the Alberta legislature. It now must pass the hurdle of full-scale debate in committee before receiving third reading and royal assent. Several opposition speakers expressed concern over undesirable factors which they said export might create . . . "Who is going to benefit chiefly from our export of gas?" asked H. J. MacDonald (Lib.-Calgary). "The Alberta government gets a yearly revenue of about $75,000 in royalties. McColl-Frontenac apparently gets $10 million. Anaconda gets cheaper gas. Do we get a trade advantage equivalent to the value of our gas?"
Mr. MacDonald said export would permit the Montana Power Company to look after the needs of Anaconda with Alberta gas and reserve its own dwindling supplies for its 33,000' residential and commercial consumers.
I mention, that to indicate the tremendous profits that are being made by these companies in the piping of oil and gas to the United States without consideration for Canadian requirements and Canadian consumers. Again I say that I hope that we from British Columbia, who have been continually fighting for an all-Canadian route by amendment of these bills to include a clause that an all-Canadian route shall be built, will be successful in the present case. To date we have been successful in the case of three other bills. I hope that other members of the house will realize that our arguments are valid and are not merely placed before the house to take up time. There are no financial difficulties in the way. There are no physical difficulties in the way. We believe it is not only the duty of members from British Columbia but the duty of members from all sides of the house to stand up and fight to preserve Canadian oil and gas for the use of Canadians first before their export is permitted from this country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank hon. members of the house for their courtesy in calling it six o'clock as early as seven or eight minutes before six. It simply meant that I did not have to introduce my speech and then put it off for a period of several hours. We are now continuing the debate on the budget. Budget night usually is a big night, but why it should be a big night I do not know because the budgets that are introduced into this house in reality are designed to perpetuate a false economic system. Yet somehow or other budgets become glorified in the minds of the people. The present monetary system under which this government and its predecessors have operated is what I call an iniquitous system. In the first place it is a debt-creating system. It is a debt and taxation system. It is a system which imposes burdens upon the people. It is a system which reduces the purchasing power of the people. It is a system which impoverishes the people, and it is a system which, carried to its conclusion, takes away the right of the people to private property. Now, why such an iniquitous monetary system should be crowned with such glory and honour is beyond my comprehension. Yet, it is so crowned.
Some of us have been sitting in this house now for a great many years. I know when I first came down to this august chamber I was inspired. I felt I was sitting in the seats of the mighty. When the budgets were brought down, surrounded with all the pomp and glory that usually accompanies budgets,
I sat rather awe-inspired. I recall, not many years after I entered this house, a previous finance minister, Mr. Dunning, brought down what was publicized as his "Mayday budget," because it was brought down on the first of May. The galleries were filled with people. The press galleries were filled with [DOT]press representatives. We sat in our seats, and1 the chamber was fairly well crowded.
The Budget-Mr. Hansell At last, the minister of finance, Mr. Dunning, entered. He was applauded. I looked at him. He was dressed in his best bib and tucker. He had on his morning coat and striped trousers. He had on his winged collar and pearl-grey tie. There he stood, in all the glory surrounding this thing we know as finance. He brought down his budget. The people listened almost spellbound. What they listened to, I do not know. I do not think they knew either. This was in what was known as the hungry thirties, and I think they were waiting for some good news. When the budget was all summed up, the only relief he was able to give the taxpayers of Canada was that he took the sales tax off gopher poison.
Now, that is the record. The other night a similar scene was enacted here. As I went to dinner at around six o'clock, the people were beginning to gather in the corridors. The constables were keeping them in line. When I came down to the chamber at approximately eight o'clock at night, the galleries were crowded with people. My telephone rang several times during the day because people were inquiring whether I could get them special tickets for the gallery. The crowds were here. We were all in our seats. I do not know why we were here, but we were here anyway. The clock struck eight. No finance minister appeared. We began to break the tension by singing a few ballads. At last, about five minutes after eight, the hon. gentleman, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), entered upon the scene. Great applause from all over the house accompanied his entrance.
My thoughts went back to one or two court trials that I have attended in my lifetime. I recall the prisoners being brought up from the cells below, stumbling in. The prisoner is placed in the prisoner's dock. He is about to hear the verdict of the jury, guilty or not guilty, and the sentence pronounced by the judge. I could not help thinking how similar the scene was on a budget night to that scene in the courtroom. Here were the people crowding to get in the galleries. I have never heard yet of prisoners, who thought perhaps they were guilty of their crime, desiring with all their might to get into the prisoner's dock to hear what their sentence was going to be. Yet that night we had the people in the galleries and the pressmen, and the minister was applauded. What for? The people were there to hear what their economic sentence was going to be for the next twelve months. What had they done to deserve this fine, this penalty? Had they committed any crimes? I fancied I saw some war veterans
23S0

The Budget-Mr. Hansell there who had fought for their country. Had they come now to receive their reward at the hands of those who managed the affairs of this country? I imagined I saw mothers there who had perhaps given sons in battle for the freedom of this country. They were all there, ears wide open, waiting to hear the penalty for their crime. After all, that is what a budget is under this present iniquitous economic system of debt and taxation.
Mr. Speaker, let me ask this. What is the purpose of an economic system? Has that ever been answered by any finance minister this country has ever had? What is the purpose of an economic system? I believe the purpose of an economic system is to allow men to enjoy the fruits of their labours. If that purpose were fully realized men could enjoy the production of the good things of the earth. If that purpose were realized, men could enjoy the good things that roll off the assembly lines or come from our factories. If that purpose were realized, men could enjoy the fruits of a modern scientific age, art, music, drama, and what have you. To obtain those things should be the purpose of an economic system. But the financial policy of this government is not designed for that purpose. The economic policies of this country are designed for everything else but the purpose for which an economic system exists. This government is more concerned with keeping this debt-creating, iniquitous financial system solvent and more concerned with the entrenchment of its vicious powers than it is over the welfare of the people. I do not think I could put it in any better words than those used by the leader of this party in the speech he gave a few days ago. As reported at page 2059 of Hansard, he said: . . . the Minister of Finance is obliged-
"Is obliged", mark you.
-to administer a financial and economic policy that compels him to be a petty dictator, because it forces him to put a much higher value on statistical figures than upon human flesh and blood.
Let us see what has taken place over the years. Many speeches in this debate have touched on the apparent shrinkage in the value of the dollar. Might I emphasize my remarks by pointing out one place in which that shrinkage is extremely evident today. Some years ago the government floated loans. They encouraged the people to buy bonds. They told the people that those bonds would always be worth 100 cents on the dollar. Even though they might be valued today at 100 cents on the dollar, we all know that that 100 cents will not buy what they used to buy when the bonds were bought. What happened was that honest people bought bonds

with honest dollars. Now those honest people are obliged to sell their bonds for dishonest dollars. A dollar is dishonest if it does not purchase the same amount of goods when it is spent as it does when it is earned. For instance, honest pensioners receiving pensions in those days now find their dollar depreciated in value. They cannot buy much more than half what they could buy in 1939.
Let me draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, an illustration or two which will perhaps bring the matter a little bit more forcibly to the attention of the house. Suppose an industry should enter into an agreement with its employees for the institution of a pension scheme. Suppose the agreement was that, if the employees paid contributions into this pension scheme, they would receive $50 a month on reaching retirement age. Then suppose that when the workers reached pensionable age and were entitled to $50 a month, the industry should pay them only $25 a month. Suppose the industry should say, "that is what we are paying you; we do not care what the agreement said." What do you suppose would' happen in a situation like that? The industry or company, as the case may be, could be brought to trial and severely penalized. Yet that is exactly what happens today, only it is the government, through its financial policy, which is the culprit.
Then again, suppose labour should contribute to a pension fund a million dollars a year, for instance. I may say that this is another illustration. Then suppose it was discovered at the end of five or ten years that the company had stolen or misappropriated half a million dollars a year. What do you suppose would happen? The officers of the company, as the case may be, could be jailed for robbery or embezzlement. The financial policies of this government have exactly the same effect as that which would1 follow if the officers of the aforementioned company had stolen half a million dollars. That is what happens today, only the government, by its financial policies, is the robber.
Let me use another illustration. I know that we all talk of dollar values and that sort of thing; but if the government does not know how to manage the financial affairs of the country, they are responsible for the depreciation in dollar value. Suppose there are two farmers-and this is a homely illustration-who are neighbours. Suppose one man gets a crop and the other man does not, and the man who does not get a crop goes over to his neighbour and says, "I have not any winter potatoes this year. Could you let me have a supply?" The farmer who had a crop would say, "Why yes, I will let you have

your winter supply of potatoes. I will give you ten sacks. You can repay me the ten sacks some other time." His neighbour thanks him very much, and takes the ten sacks of potatoes. The next winter the farmer who did not have a crop the winter before now has a nice crop and he goes over to his neighbour and says, "Neighbour, I want to pay you back the potatoes that you gave me a year ago". Then suppose when they unload the potatoes, instead of finding ten sacks there in payment for the potatoes borrowed the winter before, he finds only five sacks of potatoes there. What would you say to that? What would the farmer say to that? I know it is just a homely illustration, but the fact of the matter is that the financial policy of this government has the very same effect. What would you say to a farmer like that?

I wish hon. members would understand this. I wish those in charge of the financial policy of this country would understand it. The only way money comes into existence and gets out into circulation is through direct creation by the banking system. Nobody disputes that. And that is done by way of loans. Every bank loan means an expansion of the credit of the country, and every loan means that new money comes into existence. But every loan must be repaid. And every loan is repayable at an interest. Since all money is a statistical creation, it is impossible to pay the interest unless the interest is also created. To assume otherwise is one of the false premises upon which the present financial policy of this country is built.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have the honour of speaking in this house. I owe this high privilege to my electors who entrusted
fMr. Hansell.]
me with the pleasant duty of representing here Saguenay county, the most beautiful constituency in Canada. I might be tempted to let its attractions and wealth go unmentioned since they have become so outstanding on the American continent, but I cannot help review the physical and human forces which ushered in this glory and are destined to attend and support it, while dutifully restraining and assimilating it.
Who would have believed, twenty or even ten years ago, that this district would be the meeting point of some of the greatest financial wizards of the American continent? Who would have thought that as one of their main arguments in support of the St. Lawrence seaway, politicians would point out that it would facilitate the shipping of iron ore from this district to American steel mills? Who would have imagined that this land of Cain-so it was called in a recent national film board release-would: become the hope of the Canadian nation and a source of anxiety to the opponents of democracy?
The Saguenay, it might seem, has just discovered where its destiny lies and has proclaimed, in the face of the world, its right to existence. Conditions in Canada have, so to speak, steeped it in profound humility for four centuries. But the longer its sufferings, the more shining will be its supremacy, provided however-let us not forget this- that all concerned co-operate to give it a crown worthy of its virtues.
Saguenay county, Mr. Speaker, is that huge area of 374,950 square miles, the boundaries of which are: to the south, the river and gulf of St. Lawrence, for a distance of approximately 700 miles from Tadoussac to Blanc Sablon; to the east, the strait of Belle Isle and Newfoundland's Labrador; to the north, Ungava bay and Hudson strait; to the west, Hudson bay and James bay. Its area is equal to more than half the area of the province of Quebec and to one tenth the total area of Canada. Its geological crust, one of the oldest in the world, assumes shapes at times rugged, at times varied, at times freakish, sometimes uniform, but always spectacular.
Its climate, which is some degrees lower than that of the Quebec district, up to Sept-Iles, gets gradually cooler as one progresses northward or eastward. According to the 1941 census, this territory had a population of 28,856 inhabitants. In the 1951 census this figure will probably be close to 40,000 and it is to be expected that it will double within a few years. May I then be permitted

to express a wish. I would like the Canadian parliament, in giving the province of Quebec more adequate representation, to divide this constituency into two parts and to call the new division St. Laurent. This would serve a double purpose. It would recall two identities most dear to the hearts of all Canadians, the St. Lawrence river and the present Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent.
From a historical point of view, Saguenay county has nothing to envy the rest of this country. In Bergeronnes, my native parish, there is a monument which recalls the Basque fishermen who came here in the thirteenth century to hunt sea-lions. Other relics corroborate this fact. The discoverer of Canada, Jacques Cartier, knew of the fact and Samuel de Champlain, the founder of Quebec, christened some rivers, as his chronicles indicate. Louis Jolliet held.' a seigniory there and today a search is going on for the burial-place of that distinguished resident. Moreover, in the early days of the French colony Tadoussac was the favourite meeting-place of Ihe fur-traders. And the village of Tadoussac has preserved one of the oldest chapels in the country.
Saguenay county, Mr. Speaker, is also the county of water power. Nearly all its countless rivers have waterfalls which, if they were all developed, would produce enough power to supply the needs of American and Canadian industry. I shall mention only a few of the most important ones: Portneuf, Bersimis, Outarde, Manicouagan, Ste. Marguerite, Magpie, Romaine and St. Augustin.
It is also a fisherman's paradise. The privileged few who have had the opportunity of tasting the salmon of the Moisie river know what I mean. Trout is plentiful in its lakes, which are noteworthy for their number, their size and their colours. As for the St. Lawrence river, it supplies all the varieties of fish; caplin, smelt, halibut, cod, lobster, etc. The people east of Sept lies, with the exception now of the people of Havre St. Pierre, depend almost exclusively on fishing for their livelihood. Unfortunately, fish have not been too plentiful these last few years and the market has been unsteady. In 1949-50 the federal Department of Fisheries understood the plight of these fishermen and provided a substantial grant for which I thank the authorities. However, these people should be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits.
Furthermore, my constituency is a hunter's paradise. Who is not familiar with the mink,
The Budget-Mr. Brisson the beaver and the moose of the north shore, with the deer which gambols so graciously on Anticosti island, with the sea-lion of La Tabatiere where Mr. Louis T. Blais, of Quebec city, operates a plant for the extraction of seal oil, the only plant of its kind in the province of Quebec. Moreover a few hundred migratory birds live on these majestic islands which extend from the Mingan archipelago down to Blanc Sablon.
Besides these rivers, lakes, islands, hunters' and fishermen's paradise, there are deep and delightful bays with sandy beaches where trim villages are located. Tadoussac bay, where each summer the Canada Steamship Lines bring thousands of American tourists, is undoubtedly the best known, but there are others whose captivating charm lingers with the visitor. Seven Islands bay, for instance, one of the most beautiful, is large enough to harbour the whole British fleet. For all those reasons I have no hesitation in stating that Saguenay county is a tourists' paradise.
Saguenay is first of all a lumber country. Many of our most powerful lumber companies have set up mills and camps in that part of the country since the beginning of the last century, such as the Consolidated Paper, at Les Escoumains, Portneuf and Anticosti; the Donnacona Paper, at Sault au Mouton and Papinachois; the Anglo Pulp, at Forestville; the Quebec North Shore Paper, at Baie Comeau, Franquelin and Shelter Bay; the St. Regis Timber, at Godbout; the St. Lawrence, at Trinity Bay; the International Paper, at Pentecote; the Gulf Pulp, at Clarke City. Those companies cut more than a million cords of wood each winter and employ thousands of lumbermen. At Baie Comeau, the Quebec North Shore has one of the most modern newsprint plants in the world; this plant supplies the Chicago Tribune.
The Saguenay region is now dotted with mines. The Quebec Iron and Titanium Corporation located 200 million tons of titanium at Havre St. Pierre, near Allard lake, and built a 27 mile railroad to link the mine with Havre St. Pierre. As early as 1950, the company shipped 100,000 tons of ore to Sorel.
At Knob Lake, in northern Quebec, the Labrador Mining and Exploration Company located 281 million tons of iron ore. A 357-mile railroad will soon be built between the mine and the harbour of Sept lies. The Iron Ore Company of Canada hopes to be able in

The Budget-Mr. Brisson 1954 to ship 2,500,000 torus of ore to the steel mills.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the constituency of Saguenay is the land of the hardy pioneer who often settles on land very hard to clear. There live resourceful farmers who make the best out of what is often poor soil, provident merchants who have to build up supplies so as to meet the demand for many months and who patiently wait for incoming mail. It is the country of the confident lumberjack, who is not afraid to leave his home for months; of the stout-hearted fisherman, who has to get up in the middle of night to gather what the sea feels like bestowing upon him; of the sturdy seaman who fearlessly faces raging waves miles from shore to carry materials and supplies. There we findi the unselfish mother who courageously gives her country eight, ten, twelve or even fifteen sons and daughters; the indefatigable doctor who has to make the best of any means of transportation at his disposal so that the lives of his patients can be saved'. It is the country where the missionary epic has been written-one should read about it in Father Garnier's book "From dog-gledt to airplane"; it is also the country of the undaunted bishop who must summon up all the resources of his mind to build up an episcopal town out of thin air. The heroic apostolic vicar must face all kinds of perils to help his flock. Thousands of French-Canadians are happy to work there. It is the country of hundreds of Acadians who came from Magdalen islands, and from centres in Acadia and who have kept their ancestral traditions, not to mention hundreds of people from Newfoundland who are a credit to their native country. Finally, it is a country where hospitality is proverbial, where nothing is to be denied to the first caller, where different races as well as capital and labour compete in a friendly manner, where hundreds of Indians live in fine reserves with all due respect to His Majesty.
I congratulate the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration for the splendid residential school he has provided for the new Indian reserve of Sept lies. The school will be blessed next summer. I congratulate him also for the bill he has introduced in this house with a view to improving the conditions of the Indians. I earnestly hope that the recommendations of the Canadian episcopate regarding the education and hospitalization of those Indians will receive full consideration. I wonder also why we could not prohibit their consumption of liquor outside the reserves, since they are not allowed to use liquor within the reserves.
