Mr. Speaker, I should like to be able to convey to my English speaking colleagues some idea of the beauty and the resources of my constituency. But my knowledge of that language will not permit me to do so. For that reason I invite them to visit my constituency and I feel sure that their visit will substantiate all my claims in respect to it.
(Translation):
In that country of unrivalled beauty, why is it that tourists have barely gone farther than Tadoussac? Since fish and game are plentiful, why cannot hunters and fishermen earn their living? In that country of vast water power, why are there so few small or large industries, and in that forest land only one newsprint industry? Lumbermen flock to this district by thousands and work there six months at lumbering operations, but why will they not settle there permanently with their families? In that mining district why is it that, with the exception of Sept lies and Havre St. Pierre, people hardly benefit from the present developments? The inhabitants are vigorous people, but the sick are deprived of the benefits of modern technical developments. Why are we still without a technical or high school, and why must we send our children outside so that they may get proper schooling? Why are trade relations so difficult with the outside world? How is it that there is hardly any increase in population? In a country where people are so hospitable and so generous, why is it that, in many cases, the inhabitants of neighbouring villages hardly know each other? Why are strangers reluctant to visit there? Why is it so difficult to organize a diocese with its proper institutions? Why is it so hard to foster a regional spirit and to develop all the social works and cultural attainments that flourish elsewhere? In short, why is this constituency, blessed as it is with unlimited potentialities and1 having a history four centuries old, still in the cradle as far as its real development is concerned? Obviously, there are many reasons, but among the main ones, and I say so without hesitation, is the isolation which, even in this, the twentieth century, prevails in that district. I feel I am expressing an opinion which is deeply rooted in the hearts and minds of the vast majority of my constituents. This frustration sometimes leads to exasperation. I cannot resist the temptation of quoting a few lines from a letter I received' recently from an elector of my constituency:

The bridge is coming, but water flows under the bridge and beside it, at a time when one is sorry to be on the shore because we are so isolated. There is no road, no crossing ... no way out.
Speaking from my own experience and from that of others, how much evidence I could bring in support of this argument since I am a bona fide son of that district and the representative of that constituency. Could it be then that the government of this country have failed to do their duty?
Has not the Department of Public Works been spending millions in the Saguenay district, in the past few years, for the construction and repair of wharves? This year, the amount set aside for the construction of wharves at Tadoussac, Sept lies and Havre St. Pierre will stand at about $2 million. Does not the same department grant generous subsidies for the construction and repair of retaining walls in my constituency? I congratulate the member for Kamouraska (Mr. Masse) for having placed on the order paper a resolution, in order to call the government's attention to the erosion problem on both shores of the St. Lawrence. I support this resolution since it concerns the entire length of my constituency.
Has not the Department of Transport, for its part, built powerful and solid lighthouses to make navigation safer? I will mention but a few: Portneuf, Pointe des Monts, lie aux Oeufs, lies Cawee, lie au Perroquet, Pointe Natashquan, Cape Whittle and Table Head. Does it not, moreover, generously subsidize the Clarke Steamship Company in order that it may operate an excellent freight and passenger service between Montreal, Quebec, and Blanc Sablom, as well as the Compagnie de navigation du Bas Saint-Laurent, which operates a similar service between Rimouski or Matane, Forestville and beyond to the intermediate ports, as far as Sept lies? Does not the government, moreover, spend considerable sums of money to build modern airports, such as those in Baie Comeau and Sept lies? Has not the Compagnie de telephone du Gulfe Saint-Laurent, ever since it acquired the telegraph and telephone system in the Saguenay, also spent considerable sums of money in order to improve the service?
On the other hand, the Post Office Department is doing everything possible to ensure efficiency in transportation of mails on the north shore, by ship, plane, truck, dog-sled, etc.
But, hon. ministers, even though I thank you most sincerely for this assistance on behalf of my constituents, you know that it
The Budget-Mr. Brisson is insufficient. Every day I have occasion to ask you for a new wharf, a new retaining wall, a new airport, a new extension of the telephone system, a better steamship service or, more frequently, an improvement in the mail service. You can be sure that all those requests are legitimate and necessary, and I earnestly hope that they will be granted.
But, in my opinion, the real problem lies elsewhere. Better water and air transport between the north shore and the rest of the country will lessen the problem of its isolation, but it will not solve it. Because of its climate,

and the same goes for the rest of the province of Quebec-water and air transport will always be extraordinary means of transport. Let us admit it frankly, Saguenay county suffers from isolation in this twentieth century, simply because it has a road which is hardly practicable over a distance of 135 miles, from Tadoussac to Baie Comeau, and it has no railway.
Could it be that the provincial government has forgotten Saguenay county in its roadbuilding program, when the claim is heard all the time that the Union Nationale has given everything to the province of Quebec! Will they do something about it soon, as they say they will? Will the revenues derived from the mining rights in New Quebec be enough or do they rely on their new tax on gasoline? Be that as it may, the problem is urgent and unfortunately the provincial government of the Union Nationale is slow in solving it. If that road had been built a few years ago, Saguenay county would have surely benefited more from the new developments in New Quebec.
Should I be talking about a second trans-Canada highway in the Saguenay when so far there has been no agreement between the federal government and the Quebec government as regards the original project? It might be a good thing if the federal government, the Quebec government and the Newfoundland government got together to consider the possibility of linking Newfoundland to the mainland, by building a dam over the strait of Belle Isle which separates Blanc Sablon and Newfoundland over a distance of only nine miles. Commander Beauge has already mentioned this possibility. This project would also have a considerable and beneficial effect on the weather on both shores of the St. Lawrence, and would also constitute a valuable con-

The Budget-Mr. Brisson tribution to national defence in case of war. Let us not forget that during the two last wars, the enemy aimed their devastating projectiles at both shores of the St. Lawrence. Was that not the kind of protection the United States authorities had in mind when they built naval bases at Longue Pointe de Mingan, on the north shore, at Goose Bay, in Labrador, and at Gander in Newfoundland, during the last war?
What I really wish to ask the federal government tonight is to consider the possibility of building a railroad in the Saguenay region. The problem is directly under its jurisdiction. The member from Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais) is to be praised for placing a resolution to that effect on the order paper, early in the session. Railroads have helped the development of western provinces and strengthened our federal union. The Saguenay region could therefore also benefit in every respect from the construction of a railroad. At one time, many reasons could be given to prove the project impracticable: sparse population, lack of natural resources, technical difficulties, etc. Today such obstacles fade away in the light of the enormous development that is taking place in Ungava. If it is worth spending millions to build a railroad that will carry iron ore from Knob Lake to Sept-Iles over a distance about equal to the distance between Murray Bay and Sept-Iles; if, for the same reason, it is found advisable to complete the St. Lawrence seaway, is it not also worth spending a few millions to ensure the happiness and the well-being of the local pioneers and of the miners who will bring out this iron ore? Is it not true that the building of a railway is the only way to make available to the Canadian people the wealth and the wonders that are plentiful in that region, and would it not be the proper way to provide its population with a standard of living in keeping with our Canadian way of life? I leave this problem with the government because I am sure it will be considered with the greatest care as well as all other matters that make for a prosperous Canada.
Obviously this may not be the proper time to raise such an important question, because of the huge war expenditures with which we are faced at the present time. Under those circumstances, one cannot help regretting that constant threat of destruction we have to face when there are so many wonderful things to be accomplished at home


It is then our duty to avert the danger by strengthening our internal peace so that we may pass it on to the world, for we must not forget that international peace, like personal and national peace, can be achieved only through great sacrifices. If our country enjoys peace today, it is because our fathers made common sacrifices to build confederation, because the two great races making up our country gave up a certain pettiness in order to work towards appropriate ideals; because both capital and labour agreed to mutual sacrifices in the general interest; because the government provides social security benefits, thereby returning to the less fortunate certain taxes levied on the citizens. Let this same spirit prevail in our attempts to solve also the constitutional problems facing the ten provincial governments and the federal government, or in the closer co-operation of the two elements of our country if we wish to be soon unfettered and free. Instead of overstressing racialism and national sovereignty, nations should make greater efforts to practise charity and universal brotherhood, if salvation and not destruction of our civilization is to be attained. The Colombo plan surely came out of that principle; let us warmly congratulate the Canadian government for the generous contribution it contemplates.
In conclusion, I will express two wishes: that our government should send an ambassador to the source of peace, the Vatican, and that our very distinguished Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Horn. Lester Pearson, should continue to work for peace at the United Nations.

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) must necessarily balance the budget and of course he must raise the money required for the defence of our country. These last few years, the government announced outstanding surpluses; it must not be forgotten however that in each case they were due to increased revenues and not to reduced expenses.
It is much more difficult to go in for rigid economy when there is a surplus. Everybody knows that as one's income grows, it becomes practically impossible to refrain from spending.
Moreover, those excess revenues will eventually lead the government into committing itself to extraordinary and unforeseen expenditures. Therefore, I believe that the government should do its best to refrain from helping inflation, by avoiding such expenditures, as well as any taxes which are not strictly required to balance the budget, for taxation bears more heavily on the small taxpayer. It is well to remember that the Canadian dollar today is worth 50 cents, or only half as much as in 1939. It is true that production and salaries have increased, but one must not overlook the problems which face the head of a family who earns, for example, as does the average worker in my county, a little over $40 a week, and who wants to give his children not luxuries, but merely milk, at 18 cents a quart, meat at $1.00 a pound, not to mention rent, shoes, clothing and education.
Even if the head of a family had dreamed of buying his wife a washing machine by saving his full salary for five weeks, his dream would have quickly vanished with the new tax levied on those articles.
Nobody would complain if luxury items were the first to be taxed. Unfortunately the Minister of Finance has a strange notion of luxuries. I think he should ask the Canadian housewife who spends a whole morning cooking for the family, or doing the week's laundry in her washing machine, if these are luxury articles.
In view of the already high prices asked for such things as refrigerators, stoves and washing machines, we cannot help feeling that the new tax on those items is far too heavy.

Finally, I must protest against the fact that the government apparently wishes to protect the liquor industry. If a commodity can indeed be classed as a luxury it is that one. Experience has shown that despite all increases in the price of liquor, sales have boomed. Besides, people were expecting a tax on liquor. Indeed on the eve of the budget liquor stores were stormed by people anxious to stock up. We all know that fancy prices are hardly a deterrent to people who want their liquor.
At all events, a tax should have been levied and the minister's explanations in that connection are both lame and obscure.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I doubt very much whether the budget, and in fact the whole government program, can help curb inflation, which the Canadian people have the right to expect and are earnestly requesting. I sincerely hope that the house will support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), as I propose to do.

Mr. Speaker, before the question is put to the house I wish to make a few remarks, although it is not my intention now to make remarks that I shall make later on the main motion. As to this amendment, I wish to indicate that I believe its purpose is appropriate in view of the general effect of the budget that has been presented. It has already been said on a number of occasions-and I do not intend to repeat those arguments at the moment-that this budget bears most heavily upon those who are least able to pay any added taxes at this time. Instead of attempting to encourage saving or to ease the pressure on those who are already finding it extremely difficult to meet the greatly increased cost of living, the taxes have been so imposed that they will bear most heavily upon pensioners, upon those on smaller fixed incomes and generally upon those with the least ability to pay. That is particularly true of the sales tax which has been increased by 25 per cent of the amount previously levied. It will bear heavily on those who are already finding prices much too high on the things they need for their daily life.

Then, for reasons which have not been explained satisfactorily at any time since this budget was introduced, taxes have been imposed upon things that can only be regarded as necessities, such as stoves, refrigerators and things of that sort which today we are encouraging people to buy because of the increased rural as well as urban electrification throughout the whole of Canada. In addition to that, there is the fact that automobiles can no longer be regarded as a luxury by many of our people. In many communities today it would be impossible to carry on the ordinary occupations of the people unless many of them had automobiles in which to get to work. As a number of hon. members will know, as a result of the suddenly increased activities of defence plants many workers are driving fifteen, twenty and twenty-five miles a day to work, and some of them more. To them the automobile is a necessity. If, therefore, there were to be increases in taxes, those increases should have indicated some recognition of the difference between an automobile that is a utility, an automobile that will serve the purpose of being a conveyance to those who must have it for that purpose, and an automobile that can properly be regarded as a luxury. Therefore the whole taxing scale should have had some recognition of that fact. Go right through the budget and the same is true. There is no recognition of the fact that today the burden of the increased cost of living is bearing most heavily on those on smaller incomes, and particularly those on fixed incomes or on pensions. For that reason the surtax should not bear as heavily on those who will have the greatest difficulty in meeting those other obligations. For that reason I believe it is appropriate that the surtax should start at a higher level than that indicated in the budget. For that reason I propose to support the subamendment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this budget debate, I wish, first of all, to congratulate the Minister of Finance on his excellent work.
His budget distributes with fairness to all taxpayers the heavy burden of taxation. Of course, taxes and especially new taxes are never popular. Most people realize, however, that these taxes are rendered necessary by our rearmament. In the present international situation, the expenses to be made in this connection are the price we must pay for our freedom, for the preservation of peace and of our way of living.
In general, the budget was well received by the people. Having received no protest from my constituents in this regard, I am inclined to think it has met with their approval. On the whole, the criticisms levelled against it are unjustified. The budget, it is said, is not based on the taxpayer's ability to pay. Criticisms in this connection are directed mainly against the increased income and sales taxes. The increase in income tax, as of July 1, being 20 per cent of the present tax, is certainly based on the individual's capacity to pay. Those who, up to now, have only paid a small tax, will now pay a slightly higher tax and those who were paying a heavy tax, will have to pay even more. The new tax certainly takes into account the people's capacity to pay, since it is based on the present tax, which in turn is calculated on the taxable income after deduction of all personal exemptions to which the taxpayer is entitled.
The government is also being blamed for increasing the sales tax. It has been said that it strikes too heavily at the low income group. As stated by the Minister of Finance in his remarkable speech, the sales tax does not apply to all necessities of life. There are numerous exemptions. Ninety-five per cent of foodstuffs are exempt. All fuels and building materials are free from tax. I believe it can be said that two-thirds of the average Canadian family's expenses are not affected by the sales tax. According to a

recent survey made among people earning less than $3,000, only one-third of the total revenue is spent on goods subject to the sales tax. It is therefore incorrect to say that the sales tax is unfair and backward.
Our opponents object to the 15 per cent tax on gas and electric stoves, as well as on mechanical refrigerators and washing machines. They feel sorry for young married couples who will have to pay more for these articles. I think that their sympathy is out of place. These are luxury articles and under present conditions I believe the government did well in taxing them. The percentage of newly married couples who bought these articles, even before the new taxes, was comparatively low. As far as I am concerned, I had been married several years before I could afford the luxury of an electric stove and refrigerator; in rural districts and especially in my constituency of Iles-de-la-Madeleine, these articles are rather scarce.
Opposition members also claim that corporation taxes are too low. Right now, the two taxes on corporation profits, the federal tax and the provincial tax, absorb more than 50 per cent, 52-6 per cent to be exact, of a corporation's net profits. If the tax were to be increased further, its effect would be to discourage the investment of foreign capital in our province, a capital we badly need to develop our natural resources. The ones to suffer would be the worker and the farmer.
Indeed, if new industries are not established, if the existing industries are not expanded, that will mean so many new jobs that will not be created, so many unemployed who will not find employment and, with the resulting drop in the worker's purchasing power, the farmer will inevitably be affected since the price of agricultural products will necessarily have to drop. There are, therefore, as regards corporation taxes, certain limits which it would be dangerous to exceed.
These taxes, as I indicated earlier, are not popular. In proposing them the government has had to choose the least of many evils. The house knows, Mr. Speaker, that no government likes to impose new taxes. It is an unpleasant duty which they have to perform and which they do not relish any more than do the taxpayers who have to pay, among whom may be found, let us not forget that, the ministers themselves who impose these charges.

This duty is thrust upon them by the international situation and by the fact that free peoples find themselves obliged, much against their will, to arm themselves and to combine these armaments in order to resist communist aggression which, ever since 1945, when we thought the war had ended, has not ceased: to attack and enslave free people who were in no condition to defend themselves. This went on until the United Nations called a halt to it by going to the defence of Korea.
People who are sincere and as well informed as are the members of this house know that our own government, as well as those of our democratic allies of the second world war, had but one desire: to put an end to the armaments race, to enjoy a long period of peace, to reduce taxes and to develop our resources for the welfare and the prosperity of our people. Our government gave evidence of its peaceful intentions when it demobilized as soon as possible and sold the war material, the equipment and even the buildings it thought were no longer needed1 for national defence.
Therefore I regret, Mr. Speaker, that during this debate the government should have been taken to task for selling war material it thought would no longer be required. I am sorry too that speeches were made in this house to extol peace-as if we were not all in favour of peace-with the cynical suggestion that people are willing to pay taxes for peace activities but not for war purposes.
I mention this in passing, Mr. Speaker, because my impression is that talking like that in this house is an easy way of becoming popular with those who do not consider the situation fully, but it certainly does not help the people to accept the necessary sacrifices which we must absolutely impose upon ourselves to save from communism our liberties, our institutions and even our religion. Let us not forget how the Roman Catholic religion was persecuted in the countries behind the iron curtain. We must be realists and understand that unfortunately it is not by speaking in praise of peace that we will prevent the communists from attacking us.
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Finance presented his budget he told us he had two main objectives: the preservation of peace and the control of inflation. He told us about the steps to be taken to achieve this last objective, but he also said that the government was not ready at this time to set up price controls.
The Budget-Mr. Cannon
The Prime Minister, our respected leader, has explained the motives upon which the government based its decision. I have listened with great interest to these explanations. However, I feel I must call the attention of the government and of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) in particular to the serious effects of this decision not to impose controls, however sound it may have been, on the fishermen who constitute 85 per cent of the population of my constituency.
The cost of living has gone up in the Magdalen islands too, even more than elsewhere because of the higher cost of air or sea transport, the only way the islands can be supplied with many of the necessities of life. Fishing tackle, boats, engines, nets, fishing gear, gas and motor oil, are all a great deal more expensive. On the other hand, the price of fish is coming down and fishermen are in a difficult and very special situation.
True, the cost of living has gone up throughout the country, but for most Canadians higher costs have been at least partly offset by wage increases or, in the case of farmers, by higher prices for their products. But not so for the fishermen of the Magdalen islands. The high cost of living, combined with low prices for their fish, is almost unbearable for them and the oldest industry in Canada is in a most critical condition as a result.
Petitions signed by almost all fishermen on the islands have been sent to both the federal and provincial ministers of fisheries and their deputies. The preamble of those petitions is identical. I shall read it to the house, because it indicates the state of mind of the petitioners.
Whereas for the last few years and especially since 1945 the fishermen's condition has become so critical that their industry is expected to collapse from one season to the other. Every year an increasing number of fishermen quit their trade to earn a better living elsewhere. The fisherman cannot earn a living when his costs are greater than his income. This is very often the case since the cost of living has been increasing and the price of fish has had a tendency to decline;
Whereas the cost of living has increased at a more alarming rate here than elsewhere because of transportation charges which have doubled and even tripled during the last decade;
Whereas fishing gear has become a luxury because of its exorbitant price, making it impossible for fishermen to renew their tackle, so much so that they are now obliged to give up their trade or to operate at a loss;
In the islands, three types of fishing make up the main and practically only industry of the ten thousand inhabitants: lobster fishing, mackerel fishing and cod fishing. Since the end of the war, the price of the gear necessary for these types of fishing has doubled and even tripled, whilst the price of

The Budget-Mr. Cannon fish has declined instead of going up with the rest. Thus a lobster cage or trap which formerly sold for $1.25 now costs $2.75. A mackerel net has increased from $18 to $45 and the cod trawl has doubled in price. Everything used for fishing, from rubber clothing to gasoline, has greatly increased, while the price of fish has decreased as follows: lobster, 3 cents per pound; cod has gone down to about 2i cents a pound and mackerel in the same proportion;
Whereas the lack of balance caused by the rising prices of fishing gear and the. decrease in the price of fish greatly affect the fisherman's budget and also the economy of all the islands;
Whereas the fishing trade, while the oldest of the country, is still the least remunerative;
And whereas the fisherman believes his trade important enough to warrant the authorities' interest so that he may enjoy a living standard comparable to that of other Canadians . . .
The fishermen then request from the provincial government insurance on fishing gear and a subsidy on fishing boats.
As for the subsidy for fishing craft, the federal government's order in council P.C. 1919, dated May 22, 1947, empowers the Minister of Fisheries to pay fishermen subsidies of $165 per ton for the building of fishing craft not less than 55 feet long. This order in council authorizes the payment of these subsidies for the fishermen's benefit through fishermen's loan, boards to be set up by the provinces.
As there are, as yet, no such boards in the province of Quebec, our fishermen cannot benefit from these loans. I have already mentioned this matter in the house when. I suggested, in my speech of September 28, 1949, which is reported at page 325 of Hansard, that the provincial government set up the required organization so that the fishermen of the Magdalen islands might benefit from these subsidies.
I am happy to say that following correspondence and interviews between the federal and provincial ministers of fisheries, the federal government is now considering an amendment to the order in council so as to reduce to 45 feet the length of fishing craft eligible for the subsidies; this would meet with the views of the Quebec provincial government, which is in favour of building boats shorter than 55 feet, the length provided. I am also told that the government of the province of Quebec will establish the necessary organization so that these federal subsidies may be paid to the fishermen of Quebec province, as they are already paid to those of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
The building of larger ships would be a great boon to the fishermen, of Quebec province in general and to those of Magdalen


islands in particular. With such ships, fishermen could go further offshore, make longer trips and bring in larger hauls. I am sure that is the best solution to the fishermen's difficulties. These changes, when they come, will be a fine example of federal-provincial co-operation.
The brief presented by the fishermen to the federal government requests:
(1)	a support or floor price in line with the present cost of living;
(2)	price controls on essential fishing gear and
(3)	extension of unemployment insurance to fishermen.
Let us study these requests one by one.
As far as price support is concerned, there is a federal organization known as the fisheries prices support board. I have .had several interviews with this board and with its technical adviser.
In order to stabilize the price of fish, the board is authorized to fix a floor price. If fish is sold at a lower price, the board is empowered to pay the fisherman the difference between the floor price and the actual selling price.
I have had long interviews with the Minister of Fisheries as well as with the deputy minister and their technical advisers. I take this opportunity to thank them for the time and attention they have been so kind as to give the problems of my constituents.
There would of course be two ways of fixing a floor price, either before or after the fishing season.
I asked, Mr. Speaker, that the price be set before the beginning of the fishing season. In other words let the government guarantee the fishermen a certain minimum price fixed in advance. After the matter was thoroughly discussed and the effects of such a policy carefully considered, I was told: that if the government fixed a minimum price and guaranteed to pay the difference, if the buyers paid less than that price, the effect would be to disorganize the fish market. In fact, the buyer would naturally be inclined to pay a very low price and the fishermen would not have much to gain in asking more, for both would know that the government would pay the difference. It would be practically impossible for the government to protect itself againist the buyers ini such a case.
Furthermore in setting up a guaranteed minimum price before the marketing season

the government would hinder the marketing of fish products on the ultimate markets. In fact, these buyers knowing that the government would pay a subsidy to the fishermen to compensate them would also be tempted to pay less for the products offered to them. Such subsidies would also cause us difficulties with many countries with which we have trade agreements. The paying of subsidies would stop the exporting of our fish to many of those countries, particularly the United States-, because subsidized commodities are subject to embargo and high duties.
I therefore think it would not be practical to set up in advance a minimum price for fish.
The only solution would therefore be for the prices support board to make a payment to the fishermen at the end of the season if the prices received were not sufficient to ensure them an adequate return.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the federal government cannot make rules for the special use of the Magdalen islands. If the fisheries prices support board sets a minimum price for cod, mackerel, lobster, and so on, the price applies to all Canada, Newfoundland included. Before establishing a price, the government has to know the size of the catch in Newfoundland and the price it has fetched. The government knows the price that applied in 1950 to all parts of the country with the exception of Newfoundland where complete statistics on the catch and on the prices have never been kept. The fisheries prices support board is now making a survey of the situation in Newfoundland. As soon as the government has the figures concerning the amount of fish caught in Newfoundland and the prices which prevailed, it will decide upon the advisability of fixing a minimum price for 1950, and, if applicable, will determine the amount.
I urgently request the Minister of Fisheries to seriously consider the situation in which the fishermen in my riding find themselves, when the question of support prices for fish comes up for discussion.
According to the information I have, the fish prices support board has not yet exercised its powers to set floor prices for fish and to make payments to fishermen. I respectfully suggest to the minister that the time has come for the board to exercise those powers.
I hope, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the survey which is now being made in Newfoundland by this government will warrant setting a floor price for fish and that the
The Budget-Mr. Cannon first request of the fishermen will be granted. If the price paid in Newfoundland happens to be higher than that paid in the Magdalen islands, let the former be set as the floor price, and let the difference be paid to the islands fishermen.
The second request in the brief of the fishermen deals with price controls on fishing gear. It is unfortunately impossible to put a ceiling on prices of fishing gear without imposing general price controls, and, we all know, the government is not yet ready to take this step.
However, the budget does contain provisions to help the fishing industry. One will permit free entry of diesel engines for ships used exclusively in commercial fishing. The other will enlarge the scope of provisions already exempting from customs duties fishing nets and- fishing lines, so that they will cover nets or lines manufactured from any kind of material.
The dominion government is also doing its share in keeping the price of fishing gear as low as possible, by exempting it from the sales tax.
In its issue of April 10 last, Le Devoir published interesting figures showing the difference between the price of fishing gear in 1944 and 1950.
I have checked the list and found that the following items are exempt from tax: rope, lath for lobster cribs, lumber for boats, hand fishing lines, fish nets, barrels used for the salting of fish and motors used in fishing boats.	;
Among articles used solely by fishermen, only rubber boots and clothing as well as motor oil and gas are subject to the sales tax. I will make representations in order to have those articles exempted from the tax.
Thirdly, fishermen request unemployment insurance benefits. As early as last spring, one year ago, I made representations to the unemployment insurance commission and the Department of Labour in order to bring fishermen under the act. The unemployment insurance commission began a nationwide survey to secure the necessary information and data before reporting on this request. I understand that the report is in preparation and hope that the government will be able to include fishermen in the benefits of this legislation which has already been extended to lumberjacks.

The Budget-Mr. Cannon
If it is not possible to apply it immediately to fishermen who are not employed on a salary basis, I suggest that it be extended at least to salaried fishermen's help. That would be a first step in the right direction.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government and in particular the Minister of Fisheries will take these requests into earnest consideration.
I felt it was my duty . . .
